name: metapool
workload: Construction and reserve() of mtp::vault (pool-backed dynamic array) vs std::vector (std::allocator/ptmalloc) and std::pmr::vector (pmr pool + monotonic_buffer_resource), across element counts.
claimed_speedup: up to ~1300x faster construction/reserve than std::vector (std::allocator); up to ~3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector (pool resource)
compiler_and_flags: clang 20.1.8; -O3 -march=native -fstrict-aliasing -flto
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U, Arch Linux kernel 6.15.8, glibc 2.42 (ptmalloc), 64GB DDR5
tradeoffs: Compile-time fixed pool layout (metaset) must be tuned per workload; no general fallback beyond configured strides; header-only but requires C++23; cannot grow arbitrarily beyond the preallocated arena without a reset.
caveats: The ~1300x figure comes from a narrow construction+reserve microbenchmark (bypassing malloc/realloc growth entirely), not sustained alloc/free churn; the ~3.5x-vs-pmr figure is more representative of general use. New project (created Aug 2025), 37 stars, no independent third-party verification found.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ pool allocator faster than std::allocator benchmark github'

name: NUMAlloc
workload: PARSEC + Rodinia OpenMP/MPI multithreaded applications and Hoard-suite microbenchmarks (threadtest, larson, false-sharing) run with up to 128 threads across an 8-node NUMA machine
claimed_speedup: 15.7% faster on average than the second-best allocator (mimalloc) and 19% faster than the default Linux allocator across evaluated apps; up to 6.8x faster than Scalloc and 5.3x faster than the default allocator in the best case (fluidanimate); 2.9x faster than default / 4.6x faster than TCMalloc specifically on fluidanimate; on the Rodinia suite, 2.33x faster on average than mimalloc and 2.44x faster than the default allocator
compiler_and_flags: GCC-8.3.0, Linux Debian 10, hyperthreading off, transparent huge pages and AutoNUMA enabled, 128 threads (= core count)
hardware: Intel Xeon(R) Platinum 8153, 2.00GHz, 8 NUMA nodes x 16 physical cores (128 cores total), 512GB RAM, 32KB L1/1MB L2 per core, 22MB LLC per node
tradeoffs: About 10-12% higher memory footprint than the default allocator due to transparent-huge-page use (drops to comparable with THP disabled); designed around NUMA-aware node/thread binding, so benefits are largest on multi-socket/multi-node machines and smaller on single-socket systems; needs origin-aware object return and an interleaved heap that can hurt serial-phase-heavy applications.
caveats: Repo has no top-level LICENSE file even though the SC'22 paper text says the code 'will be opened source using GNU GPL V2 license... upon acceptance' -- treat as unclear/no license (usability=reference) rather than assuming GPL-2.0. The repository bundles source and papers for roughly 10 different UTSASRG projects (SC22, ISMM22/23, EuroSys22/23, HPCA22, OOPSLA20/21, TPDS, plus a patent folder), so which exact source subfolder is 'the' released NUMAlloc build is not obvious from the repo alone. Last push 2023-03-01 (>3 years ago), so treated as abandoned.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'memory allocator faster than std::allocator malloc evaluation paper' -> gh search repos "numalloc" -> UTSASRG/numalloc SC2022/evaluation.tex, abstract.tex, intro.tex

name: SuperMalloc
baseline: best of DLmalloc, JEmalloc, Hoard, and TBBmalloc
workload: malloc-test multithreaded allocate/free microbenchmark at 1, 8 (with hardware transactional memory), and 32 threads on 64-bit Linux
claimed_speedup: ~2.1x faster than the best of DLmalloc/JEmalloc/Hoard/TBBmalloc with 1 thread; 2.75x faster with 8 threads + HTM; 3.4x faster with 32 threads (no HTM)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.3 on Linux 3.15.7 / glibc 2.18 (Fedora 20); also uses Haswell hardware transactional memory (HTM) intrinsics for the lock-elision fast path
hardware: 4-core i7-4770 (Haswell-DT, 3.4GHz, 1 socket + hyperthreading) for the HTM results; 16-core 2-socket 2.4GHz Xeon-class machine for the larger-thread-count results
tradeoffs: Full-speed path requires Haswell+ hardware transactional memory; ships a separate pthread-lock build (libsupermalloc_pthread.so) for machines without HTM. Uses more virtual address space via a superblock design. Author Bradley Kuszmaul's ISMM'15 paper implementation, not a maintained production allocator.
caveats: Benchmark toolchain (gcc 4.8.3 / glibc 2.18 / Fedora 20) is from 2015; repo has had no commits since 2019-11-15 so there is no recent head-to-head vs jemalloc/mimalloc/snmalloc/rpmalloc. Numbers come from the project's own malloc-test benchmark (bundled in the same repo as the paper source), not an independent third party, but compiler, flags-equivalent build config, and exact CPU models are all stated in the paper text, so it meets tier A.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch '"SuperMalloc" OR "scalloc" OR "Mesh allocator" benchmark faster than jemalloc tcmalloc paper' -> gh search repos "supermalloc" -> repo paper/ismm15/supermalloc.tex

name: Hoard
baseline: Solaris default allocator, Ptmalloc (glibc malloc backing operator new/delete)
workload: Uniprocessor and multiprocessor (1-14 way Sun Enterprise 5000) allocation-intensive benchmarks: threadtest, shbench, Larson server simulation, active/passive false-sharing tests, BEMengine PDE solver, Barnes-Hut n-body solver, plus single-threaded espresso/Ghostscript/LRUsim/p2c.
claimed_speedup: Up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator and up to 18x over the next-best allocator (Ptmalloc) at 14 processors (paper abstract); threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; BEMengine 10.6% faster than Solaris allocator uniprocessor
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ at -O6 (Sun Workshop C++ compiler 5.0 used only for Barnes-Hut)
hardware: Sun Enterprise 5000, 2GB RAM, 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC CPUs, 4MB L2 cache, Solaris 7
stars_or_usage: 1.25k stars; historically used by AOL, Cisco, SAP, Reuters, RBC and others per README; standard allocator option in SPEC CPU2006
tradeoffs: Multi-heap design trades some memory for scalability (bounded blowup, not zero); link-time/LD_PRELOAD drop-in malloc replacement, not a std::allocator template adapter; per-processor heap hashing can cause heap/thread collisions.
caveats: Primary quantitative evidence is a peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2000 paper run on 26-year-old hardware (UltraSPARC/Solaris 7) against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era, not a modern libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL build; no current reproduction with stated modern compiler/flags/hardware was found this session, so capped at Tier B rather than A. The GitHub repo itself is actively maintained in 2026 as a drop-in malloc replacement, and Hoard is also included (as 'hd') in the independent daanx/mimalloc-bench suite, though that page's results are chart images only, not text numbers.
found_via: GitHub: found via daanx/mimalloc-bench README allocator list ('hd' = Hoard); followed citation to the ASPLOS 2000 paper

name: scalloc
baseline: ptmalloc2 (glibc's default malloc, part of GNU libc; extends Doug Lea's dlmalloc)
workload: SPEC CPU2006 483.xalancbmk single-threaded allocation-intensive workload, plus threadtest/shbench/larson multithreaded microbenchmarks and an ACDC-generated producer-consumer workload
claimed_speedup: ~1.33x SPEC ratio vs ptmalloc2 on single-threaded 483.xalancbmk (Figure 5, on par with TCMalloc's ~1.34x); among the fastest and most memory-efficient allocators (previously TBB was fastest) across the multithreaded threadtest/shbench/larson suite
hardware: UMA machine, 4x 10-core 2GHz Intel Xeon E7-4850 (2 hardware threads/core), 32KB L1D, 32KB L1I, 256KB L2/core, 24MB L3/processor, 128GB RAM, Linux kernel 3.8.0
tradeoffs: Reserves up to 32TB of virtual address space per arena (relies on on-demand paging / madvise to keep physical memory low); distributed via LD_PRELOAD on Linux / DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES on OSX; needs overcommit accounting and transparent-huge-pages tuned for best results.
caveats: OOPSLA'15 paper (arXiv v2, Aug 2015) is now 10+ years old; the current repo README says the allocator was 'completely rewritten from scratch' since the paper and points benchmarking at a separate cksystemsgroup/scalloc-artifact repo that has not been updated since 2019, so today's numbers may differ from the paper's. Exact compiler/version and optimization flags used for the SPEC run were not found in the extracted paper text, so tier is capped at B rather than A.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch '"SuperMalloc" OR "scalloc" OR "Mesh allocator" benchmark faster than jemalloc tcmalloc paper' -> gh search repos "scalloc" -> arxiv.org/pdf/1503.09006

name: arena-allocator (ShortAlloc)
baseline: operator new/delete (GNU/glibc malloc via std::vector's default std::allocator)
workload: std::vector<TestClass>::emplace_back of 100 objects of sizes 8B-8KB, using a stack-backed bump-pointer Arena + ShortAlloc STL allocator vs the default heap allocator, measured on QuickBench (AWS-hosted).
claimed_speedup: Stack/arena allocator 2.2x-4.4x faster for objects up to 512B, and 93x-230x faster for 1KB-8KB objects (crossing glibc's mmap threshold)
hardware: QuickBench-hosted AWS machine pool; CPU model and load unstated (README includes explicit disclaimer that absolute QuickBench timings are unreliable)
stars_or_usage: 9 stars; featured in a Hacker News 'Show HN' post
tradeoffs: Bump allocator: cannot free individual objects out of order, only the whole arena at once (or most-recent-first); backed by a fixed-size std::array, so capacity is bounded by the configured arena size; not thread-safe.
caveats: Compiler and optimization flags are not stated, and several ratios (93x-230x) exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, coinciding with crossing glibc's mmap allocation threshold (a known artifact of that one size range, not a general allocator speed claim) -- capped at Tier C rather than A. QuickBench's own disclaimer says absolute durations on its shared AWS pool are 'meaningless' beyond relative comparison. No LICENSE file in the repo, so usability is 'reference' only, not 'copyable'.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'arena allocator C++ github faster than operator new' -> Hacker News 'Show HN: C++ Arena Allocator That's 200x+ Faster Than GNU Malloc'

name: arena-allocator (yaroslavaristov)
workload: Sequential allocation of 1-1024 fixed-size objects and a mixed small/medium/large-object batch, arena bump-pointer vs plain malloc
claimed_speedup: 10x-27x faster sequential allocation than malloc on AMD EPYC 7763 (N=1 to 1024 objects), 15x faster on a mixed-size batch; on Apple M1 (virtualized) 32x-342x faster sequential allocation and 15x on the mixed batch
compiler_and_flags: Release build, -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -Wall -Wextra -Werror -DNDEBUG (compiler name/version not stated)
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (GitHub Codespaces, x86_64, native); Apple M1 (aarch64, via OrbStack virtualization -- author notes 'not native hardware')
tradeoffs: Bump-pointer only: no per-object free, just a bulk reset(); fixed power-of-two capacity decided at construction; not a general-purpose allocator (no fragmentation handling, no shrink/grow); single header, single contributor, unaudited.
caveats: Very new (pushed within the last ~2 months), 1-star personal project, not peer reviewed. The largest claimed multiples (97x-342x on Apple M1) were measured on virtualized (OrbStack) hardware that the README itself calls non-native/unreliable, and exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, so tier is capped at C rather than A/B despite stated compiler flags and hardware. Comparing a no-free bump allocator against general-purpose malloc is a favorable, narrow workload (arena wins almost by construction once frees are removed from the critical path).
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: gh search repos "arena allocator" "faster than malloc"

name: Lockless Memory Allocator
baseline: glibc malloc (ptmalloc, the built-in allocator of Ruby 2.6.5 and 2.5.1 on Linux); jemalloc and tcmalloc also run
workload: Third-party Ruby allocation stress script (12 million small string allocations with 600,000 retained and periodic large allocations up to 100 KB), run with LD_PRELOAD of each allocator, wall seconds and peak RSS, for 1 and 8 threads.
claimed_speedup: SamSaffron/allocator_bench (Ruby 2.6.5, lockless 1.4 versus built-in glibc malloc): 8 threads 2.859 s versus 3.423 s (1.20x faster, derived from page data) with RSS 249,540 KB versus 186,336 KB (34% more); 1 thread 2.874 s versus 3.296 s (1.15x faster) with RSS 164,468 KB versus 169,444 KB. Older run (Ruby 2.5.1): 3.568 s versus 4.928 s (1.38x). Versus jemalloc 5.2.1 the same runs are within about 2% (2.859 s versus 2.922 s at 8 threads; 2.874 s versus 2.931 s at 1 thread), and tcmalloc 2.6.3 is faster single-threaded (2.526 s). The vendor's own page (not opened, blocked) is quoted in search snippets as 'everywhere faster than the glibc allocator, sometimes by more than an order of magnitude'.
stars_or_usage: benchmark repo (allocator_bench) has 56 stars; no stars figure for the vendor site
tradeoffs: Preload or link replacement of malloc; the benchmark shows a larger memory footprint than glibc (about 34% higher RSS at 8 threads) and Percona's MySQL test is quoted in search snippets as showing over 5 GB RSS for mysqld. GPL (with a commercial licence sold by the vendor) rules out some uses.
caveats: Evidence is one personal Ruby benchmark repo (code public, last commit 2020-07-06) with no CPU model, compiler or flags stated, so tier C; the results are single runs without variance. The vendor page https://locklessinc.com/benchmarks_allocator.shtml and the vendor site itself were egress-blocked, so the vendor numbers (compared with eglibc 2.11, nedmalloc 1.06, hoard 3.8, jemalloc 2.2.1, tcmalloc 1.7 per a search snippet) could not be checked, and licence (GPL-3.0-or-later), source availability and last release come from the awesome-c listing and the benchmark README's 'make' instructions, not from the vendor site. The Ruby workload is dominated by Ruby, so the allocator margin is small (1.0 to 1.4x). Version tested is lockless 1.4 (the benchmark repo date suggests around 2019-2020).
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: awesome-c Memory-Management listing of Lockless Memory Allocator, then web searches for 'Lockless memory allocator benchmark' that surfaced https://github.com/SamSaffron/allocator_bench

name: ltalloc
workload: Same multi-threaded small-object alloc/dealloc stress test used in the smmalloc benchmark table (Windows/i7-2600 and PS4), comparing ltalloc's throughput against CRT malloc.
claimed_speedup: ~2.6x faster than CRT single-threaded (62.5M vs 23.9M ops) on i7-2600; ~6.4x faster than CRT single-threaded on PS4 (28.6M vs 4.4M ops)
hardware: Windows 10, Intel Core i7-2600; PlayStation 4
tradeoffs: Overrides global operator new/delete directly (not a std::allocator wrapper); best suited for many small (<256B) allocations; peak performance relies on LTO/inlining of the size-class computation.
caveats: Numbers are from a third-party project's (smmalloc) own comparison table, not from ltalloc's own README, which has no quantified benchmark of its own (only asm-output examples). Hardware is stated but compiler/flags are not, capping this at Tier C. Despite the 'r-lyeh-archived' org name and GitHub 'archived' fork lineage, the repo has commits in 2026 and is not GitHub-archived.
found_via: GitHub: harvested from SergeyMakeev/smmalloc README benchmark table while researching smmalloc

name: rpmalloc
baseline: operator new/delete (default malloc); also compared against tcmalloc, jemalloc, lockfree-malloc, Hoard, ptmalloc3
workload: Multi-threaded interleaved allocation/deallocation benchmark (random and fixed sizes 16B-160000B range, with cross-thread deallocation), measuring memory operations per CPU-second across thread counts.
claimed_speedup: rpmalloc faster than all tested allocators except lockfree-malloc in some high-thread-count cases; tcmalloc and jemalloc trail ~15% behind in performance
hardware: 8-core (4 physical + HT) Windows 10 / Linux (Ubuntu 16.10) machine, 12GiB RAM; 2-core MacBook, 8GiB RAM for macOS (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Malloc replacement (override new/delete or LD_PRELOAD), not a std::allocator template; thread-caching adds roughly 10-15% memory overhead vs some allocators.
caveats: Benchmark is the project's own suite; exact CPU model is not named (only core count/RAM), and compiler/optimization flags are not stated in BENCHMARKS.md, so capped at Tier C. Also appears as a strong performer in the independent daanx/mimalloc-bench suite (as 'rp'), though that page's numeric results are only in chart images, not text.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'rpmalloc benchmark vs malloc vs mimalloc vs tcmalloc github'

name: smmalloc
workload: Multi-threaded (1-5 threads on Windows/i7-2600; 1-4 threads on PS4) small-object alloc/dealloc stress test measuring total operations completed, comparing smmalloc against CRT malloc, rpmalloc, Hoard, ltalloc, dlmalloc.
claimed_speedup: ~40 cycles/op with thread cache; ~3.9x faster than CRT single-threaded (92.6M vs 23.9M ops) and ~2.6x faster at 5 threads (38.3M vs 14.6M ops) on i7-2600; ~8.1x faster than CRT single-threaded on PS4 (36.1M vs 4.4M ops)
hardware: Windows 10, Intel Core i7-2600; PlayStation 4
stars_or_usage: 335 stars; shipped in Warface (PS4, Xbox One, Switch)
tradeoffs: Proxy allocator: only handles configured small-size buckets, passes everything else through to a fallback allocator; requires explicit per-thread cache create/destroy calls; not a drop-in std::allocator without a wrapper.
caveats: README benchmark states hardware but not compiler or optimization flags, so capped at Tier C rather than A/B; numbers are raw op counts from the project's own charts/tables, not independently reproduced. No commits since 2023.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'smmalloc SergeyMakeev small object allocator benchmark faster than malloc'

name: SpeedMalloc
baseline: jemalloc (also compared against TCMalloc, mimalloc, Mallacc, Memento)
workload: Multi-threaded allocation-heavy workloads used to evaluate a proposed lightweight programmable core for memory allocation offload (specific benchmark suite not given in the abstract)
claimed_speedup: 1.75x over jemalloc, 1.18x over TCMalloc, 1.15x over mimalloc, 1.23x over Mallacc, 1.18x over Memento on multi-threaded workloads
tradeoffs: Relies on a proposed lightweight programmable core embedded in the memory system to keep allocator metadata off the main cores and reduce cache conflicts -- this is a hardware/software co-design, not a software-only drop-in allocator, so it cannot be used on commodity CPUs as-is.
caveats: arXiv preprint (Aug 2025), no linked code or artifact repository found. Only compares against other custom allocators (jemalloc, TCMalloc, mimalloc, Mallacc, Memento), never against std::allocator, raw malloc, or glibc directly. Included per the 'papers with no code' rule for the research section; has_code=false and usability=reference reflect that it cannot currently be used.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'memory allocator faster than std::allocator malloc evaluation paper' -> arxiv.org/abs/2508.20253

name: Boost.Fiber
workload: skynet microbenchmark (ported from atemerev/skynet): spawn 10 threads-of-execution recursively until 1,000,000 total actors/fibers are created (only 10,000 for std::thread/std::async/pthread due to resource exhaustion); each returns its ordinal number, summed back up to the root; average time-per-unit measured with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock
claimed_speedup: fiber (16C/32T, work-stealing scheduler, tcmalloc): 0.05-0.09 microseconds/fiber vs std::thread 52-73 microseconds/thread and std::async 106-122 microseconds/thread over 10,000 units (~600-1400x lower time-per-unit; derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: gcc-6.3.1, variant=release, optimization=speed
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620v4 2.2GHz, 16 cores/32 threads, 64GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 511 stars on the standalone mirror; ships as part of the Boost C++ Libraries collection used industry-wide
tradeoffs: Cooperative user-space scheduling: a blocking syscall or CPU-bound fiber can stall all fibers on its worker thread unless paired with async I/O (e.g. Boost.Asio integration); best numbers require a non-default allocator (tcmalloc) and a work-stealing scheduler configuration; different programming model (fiber-per-task) than raw std::thread/std::async call sites.
caveats: Numbers come from Boost's own project documentation (first party), though the benchmark code itself (performance/thread/skynet_std.cpp and the fiber counterpart in the same repo) is public and the compiler/flags/hardware are all stated, meeting the tier-A bar despite the source being first-party. The raw ratio (>50x) looks extreme, but it is explained by mechanism (fiber creation/context switch avoids syscalls and stack-guard-page setup that std::thread/std::async incur) rather than a flawed methodology; std::thread could only be tested at 10,000 units instead of 1,000,000 due to OS resource exhaustion, so the two are not run at identical scale. Measurements were taken with gcc-6.3.1, an old compiler (circa 2017); the fiber library and hardware landscape have moved on since, and the doc gives no indication the numbers were re-run on newer toolchains.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh api search/code "skynet repo:boostorg/fiber"; doc/performance.qbk read via gh api raw content

name: dispenso
workload: "summing_for" parallel-for microbenchmark summing 1M and 100M elements, swept 1-166 threads on a 166-core AMD EPYC Genoa server; dispenso::parallel_for vs tbb::parallel_for.
claimed_speedup: 1M elements, 1 thread: 279us (dispenso) vs 450us (tbb) = 1.61x; 1M elements, 8 threads: 50.6us vs 175.8us = 3.48x; 100M elements, 16 threads: 2.27ms vs 3.47ms = 1.53x (all derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: GNU 11.5.0, C++20, CMake Release build (cxx_flags: -I/tmp/folly-shim); explicit -O level not separately listed
hardware: AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor, 166 cores, 224 GB RAM, Linux 6.16.1
stars_or_usage: 305 stars; used in hundreds of projects at Meta
tradeoffs: Larger API surface than std::async (work-stealing pools, parallel_for, futures, task graphs, concurrent containers); explicitly positioned as a TBB/OpenMP alternative rather than a drop-in std::async replacement.
caveats: The README explicitly advertises a benchmark of dispenso vs std::async ('Future/Async Tree Build Benchmark' suite, comparing against OpenMP, TBB, TaskFlow, folly, and std::async), but the live interactive dashboard's embedded data for that specific chart is empty (zero data points) on all four tested platforms, so no std::async claim could be verified this session -- only the TBB comparison (used above) has real numbers. Very small workloads (e.g. summing_for at 1000 elements) show >50x gaps that look like measurement/dispatch-overhead artifacts and were excluded in favor of the 1M/100M element results.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than std::async" surfaced facebookincubator/dispenso README mention of std::async benchmarks; numbers extracted from the PLATFORMS JSON embedded in docs/benchmarks/index.html

name: TooManyCooks (TMC)
workload: Recursive fork-join microbenchmarks (skynet 100M tasks, nqueens, fib(39), matmul(2048)) on a 64-core/64-thread AMD EPYC 7742 server, no SMT.
claimed_speedup: 3.77x faster than oneTBB on skynet (37,949us vs 142,887us); 1.79x on nqueens; 2.49x on fib(39); 1.12x on matmul(2048); mean-ratio-to-best across the four workloads: 1.32x (TMC) vs 3.25x (oneTBB) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.7, Release, -O3 -march=native
hardware: AMD EPYC 7742 64-core processor, 64 worker threads (no SMT), Debian 13 Server, linked against libtcmalloc_minimal.so.4
tradeoffs: Requires C++20 coroutines; Clang recommended (best coroutine codegen), MSVC unsupported due to a compiler bug; optional hwloc dependency for NUMA-aware scheduling; steeper API than std::async.
caveats: The benchmark suite (tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks, 36 stars, license NOASSERTION) is maintained by the same author as TooManyCooks, so it is not a fully independent third party, though the code, compiler, flags, and CPU model are all public and reproducible. Baseline beaten is oneTBB, not std::async/std::thread/std::future directly; no head-to-head benchmark against raw std::async/std::thread was located for this project.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "thread pool faster than std::async" --sort stars; then README link to github.com/tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks

name: utl::parallel (UTL ThreadPool)
workload: Four microbenchmark scenarios, 1000 tasks each: (1) small non-recursive tasks busy-waiting 0-100us, (2) large non-recursive tasks busy-waiting 1000-3000us, (3) shallow recursive tasks (0-100us with 70% chance of spawning+awaiting one more such task), (4) deep recursive tasks (0-100us with 49% chance of spawning+awaiting two more such tasks, averaging ~50 subtasks); reports ms/op and op/s relative to a serial baseline
claimed_speedup: Small non-recursive: utl::parallel::ThreadPool 573.3% vs std::async() 214.0% of serial speed (~2.7x faster than std::async, derived from page data). Large non-recursive: 597.0% vs 564.2% (~1.06x, roughly tied). Shallow recursive: 583.0% vs 161.1% (~3.6x faster than std::async; BS::thread_pool and progschj/ThreadPool deadlock entirely on this workload). Deep recursive: 565.1% vs 154.7% (~3.65x faster than std::async, derived from page data).
hardware: 6-core AMD Ryzen 5 5600H, hyper-threading disabled
tradeoffs: Uses a custom future type instead of std::future so recursive awaiting doesn't deadlock, so it is not a drop-in std::future replacement; ships as one module inside a larger multi-module header-only utility collection (UTL) rather than a standalone package; explicitly a niche tool for recursive/scatter-gather workloads, not a general vendor-optimized scheduler like TBB/OpenMP.
caveats: Author explicitly disclaims superiority over vendor-optimized frameworks (OpenMP/TBB). On large non-recursive tasks the advantage over std::async almost disappears (~1.06x) since thread-creation overhead is amortized; the large speedups are concentrated in small-task and recursive-task scenarios, exactly where std::async's per-call thread-spawn cost dominates. Benchmarked on a single consumer laptop CPU (Ryzen 5 5600H), not server-class hardware; this is the project's own README benchmark with no independent third-party reproduction found, though code, compiler, flags, and CPU model are all public and stated (meets Tier A bar on reproducibility grounds). Library itself is small (336 stars) and young.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia search "thread pool std async" surfaced "Show HN: Utl:parallel - Work-stealing concurrency library for C++17" (4 points, 2025-08-03) -> https://github.com/DmitriBogdanov/UTL/blob/master/docs/module_parallel.md, opened directly

name: Taskflow
workload: Large-scale machine-learning task graph (heterogeneous CPU+GPU pipeline) executed via Taskflow's executor vs. oneTBB's FlowGraph on a 40-CPU, 4-GPU machine
claimed_speedup: up to 29% faster runtime, 1.5x less memory, and 1.9x higher throughput than oneTBB on the ML workload
hardware: 40 CPUs, 4 GPUs (specific CPU/GPU model not stated in the abstract)
tradeoffs: Header-only but requires C++17/20; DAG/graph-based task model differs from raw std::async/std::thread call sites, so adopting it means restructuring code around tf::Taskflow/tf::Executor; larger API surface than a simple thread pool.
caveats: This benchmark measures Taskflow against Intel oneTBB, not against std::async/std::thread/std::future directly (oneTBB is itself already catalogued separately as a faster-than-std library, so this shows Taskflow beating another fast library, one step removed from the raw std baseline). GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION for this repo, but the LICENSE file text is the standard MIT license. Compiler/flags for the ML benchmark are not stated in the abstract, only CPU/GPU counts, so tier is capped at B rather than A. The repo's own benchmarks/ directory (thread_pool, graph_traversal, wavefront, etc.) additionally compares Taskflow to OpenMP tasking and TBB FlowGraph, not to std::async/thread.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): gh search repos "taskflow" --sort stars; README review; arXiv abstract 2004.10908 (IEEE TPDS 2021/2022 paper) opened via WebFetch

name: libfork
baseline: oneTBB (Intel Threading Building Blocks) and OpenMP (libomp)
workload: Fork-join fibonacci and unbalanced-tree-search (T3L) style benchmarks measuring task spawn/run overhead and peak memory, swept across 1-112 cores per the accompanying paper.

name: BS::thread_pool
workload: General motivational claim (README "Motivation" section): std::thread creates a new OS thread per call with significant overhead; no direct numeric std::thread-vs-pool micro-benchmark is published. The only quantified benchmark is single- vs multi-threaded Mandelbrot-set rendering using the pool itself (24.2x speedup on a 32-thread Intel i9-13900K, MSVC C++23 /O2), which measures multithreading efficiency, not std::thread/std::async overhead directly.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only ("std::thread ... can have a significant performance overhead"); no specific ratio vs std::thread or std::async is given anywhere in the documentation
stars_or_usage: 3,054 stars; also published in SoftwareX (DOI 10.1016/j.softx.2024.101687) and as arXiv:2105.00613

caveats: Included as the single Tier-D entry for this run: the project is highly notable (3k+ stars, peer-reviewed companion paper) and its entire premise is beating std::thread's per-task overhead, but no page found in this session states an actual measured std::thread-vs-pool number -- only the unrelated Mandelbrot single-vs-multithreaded speedup is quantified.

name: KANN
baseline: Theano 0.8.2 + Keras 1.2.2 (CPU, MKL); also TensorFlow 1.0.0 (CPU) and tiny-dnn
workload: Training time on CPU for small networks: mnist-mlp (one hidden layer of 64 neurons), mnist-cnn (two 3x3x32 conv layers, max pool, 128-neuron dense), mul100-rnn (two GRU layers of size 160, 30000 samples), each run for a fixed number of epochs.
claimed_speedup: mnist-mlp, Linux 1 CPU: KANN+SSE 31.3 s, KANN+BLAS 18.8 s versus Theano+Keras 33.7 s (1.8x for BLAS, derived from page data) and Tiny-dnn 2m19s (4.4x for SSE, derived). Mac 1 CPU: KANN 27.1 s versus TensorFlow 33.4 s and Theano+Keras 37.2 s. mul100-rnn, Linux 4 CPUs: KANN+SSE 12m13s and KANN+BLAS 8m18s versus Theano+Keras 19m52s (1.6x and 2.4x, derived). mnist-cnn 4 CPUs: KANN 19m09s versus Theano+Keras 24m24s; mnist-cnn 1 CPU: KANN 57m57s versus Tiny-dnn+AVX 300m40s (5.2x, derived) but KANN is slower than Theano+Keras there (37m12s).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README runs; the repo Makefile defaults to 'gcc -g -Wall -Wextra -Wc++-compat -O2'; KANN+BLAS used OpenBLAS-0.2.19
hardware: Linux: 48 cores on two Xeon E5-2697 CPUs at 2.7GHz (plus a Tesla K40c used only for the Keras GPU row); Mac: Core i7-3667U 2GHz, 4 cores
tradeoffs: Four source files (kautodiff, kann), under 4000 lines, only the C library by default, optional OpenBLAS and pthreads. CPU only, no batch normalization or other common operators, verbose RNN training API, not meant for large networks. Benchmarks cover small networks only.
caveats: First-party numbers from 2017 (Theano 0.8.2, Keras 1.2.2, TensorFlow 1.0.0, Tiny-dnn pulled March 1 2017), long before current frameworks; compiler version and flags used for the README runs are not stated, so tier C although the competitor scripts are in the repo (examples/keras, examples/tensorflow, examples/tiny-dnn). The README itself says to not read too much into the table, that Theano is about 50% faster than KANN single-threaded on mnist-cnn because of MKL sgemm, and that MKL/OpenBLAS matmul can be twice as fast as KANN's own. The wins are against Tiny-dnn and Theano/Keras on specific rows, and the KANN+BLAS rows add OpenBLAS, so the claim is not that KANN's own kernels beat MKL. None of the baselines are in the category's incumbent list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor).

name: MessagePack (msgpack-c)
workload: Encode and tree-parse randomly generated schemaless objects (2,367 bytes small and 248,571 bytes large as MessagePack; 3,183 and 308,908 bytes as minified JSON), result hash time subtracted, best and worst of 7 ten-second runs dropped.
claimed_speedup: ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks, AMD Phenom II X6 1090T, microseconds per iteration. Write, small: msgpack C++ 2.77 and msgpack C 6.42 versus RapidJSON 12.26 (4.4x and 1.9x, derived from page data); write, large: 347.14 and 544.24 versus 1097.71 (3.2x and 2.0x). Tree parse, small: msgpack C 6.47 and C++ 9.40 versus RapidJSON in-situ 10.58 (1.6x and 1.1x); tree parse, large: 750.87 and 1004.67 versus 1129.46 (1.5x and 1.1x). Raspberry Pi (ARMv6) write, small: 38.36 and 69.21 versus 231.33 (6.0x and 3.3x). The project's own README only says 'It's like JSON but smaller and faster' with no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3.0 on Arch Linux, -Wall -O3 -flto -fno-fat-lto-objects -DPIC -fPIC -DNDEBUG
hardware: AMD Phenom II X6 1090T desktop (x86_64); also a Raspberry Pi with ARMv6 rev 7
tradeoffs: Binary and not human-readable; the format is smaller (2,367 versus 3,183 bytes for the small data set). The same suite shows MPack (the benchmark author's library) faster than msgpack-c in every row (write small 2.13 versus 2.77 us), and the msgpack C++ unpacker compiles larger than RapidJSON (19,152 versus 14,600 bytes).
caveats: The benchmark was written by the author of competing library MPack, who discloses possible bias. It measures format plus library together (binary versus text), against RapidJSON 1.0.2 and msgpack-c 1.3.0 from January 2016 (the repo's last commit), while msgpack-c is now at 9.0.0. The tree-parse win is thin for the C++ API (about 1.1x) and msgpack-c C is the faster of the two. Against protobuf, the baseline the lead suggested, msgpack is not faster: thekvs/cpp-serializers (Intel Core i7, Ubuntu 16.04, msgpack 3.1.1, protobuf 3.7.0, 1,000,000 round trips) reports msgpack 2560.6 ms versus protobuf 2312.78 ms (protobuf 1.11x faster) but msgpack smaller (13,402 versus 16,116 bytes). Other sources not checked: the Apache Fory C++ benchmark page and reflect-cpp benchmark images carry msgpack rows but their numbers were not reachable.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: awesome-cpp Serialization listing of MessagePack, then https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-c and a web search for 'msgpack-c benchmark vs rapidjson' that surfaced ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks; cross-checked with thekvs/cpp-serializers

name: fbthrift
baseline: Protocol Buffers C++ (protobuf; version not stated), measured with SerializeToArray, SerializeAsString and SerializeToZeroCopyStream
workload: folly::Benchmark microbenchmark in thrift/lib/cpp2/protocol/benchmark: serialize and deserialize a struct of repeated field groups (i32, i64, 8-byte string, list<i32> of 10, map<string,i32> of 5, bool, double) in Small (1 group), Medium (3 groups) and Large (9 groups) sizes, Thrift Binary, Compact and cursor-based (CurSe) protocols against Protobuf equivalents (and an internal Carbon format).
claimed_speedup: Header comment 'Results for last run: 2025-11-18', time per iteration. Serialize Small: Thrift Binary 380.11 ns, Compact 395.36 ns, CurSe 230.85 ns versus Protobuf Array 945.69 ns, String 832.30 ns, ZeroCopy 998.08 ns (Binary about 2.2-2.6x faster, CurSe about 3.6-4.3x, derived from page data). Serialize Medium: Binary 936.16 ns, Compact 948.40 ns, CurSe 456.09 ns versus Protobuf 2.94 us / 2.55 us / 3.04 us (Binary about 2.7-3.2x). Serialize Large: Binary 2.72 us, Compact 2.75 us, CurSe 1.23 us versus Protobuf 9.54 us / 8.32 us / 9.60 us (Binary about 3.1-3.5x). Deserialize Small: Binary 396.13 ns, Compact 424.35 ns versus Protobuf about 660.7-681.1 ns (about 1.6-1.7x). Deserialize Medium: Binary 1.06 us, Compact 1.10 us versus Protobuf 2.08-2.18 us (about 1.9-2.1x). Deserialize Large: Binary 3.15 us, Compact 3.29 us versus Protobuf 6.58-6.68 us (about 2.0-2.1x).
compiler_and_flags: buck2 mode opt-clang-lto (Meta-internal fbcode build; clang version and protobuf version not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires the folly dependency stack and the Thrift compiler and IDL, which is a heavier build than protobuf; fbthrift diverged from Apache Thrift with its own cpp2 code generator, field_ref API, adapters and CursorBasedSerializer. Wire formats differ (Thrift Binary/Compact are larger or comparable but not identical to protobuf varint encoding).
caveats: First-party results pasted into a source comment (dated 2025-11-18); the benchmark code is public but CPU model, core count, clang and protobuf versions are not stated, and it needs the Meta fbcode/buck build, so it is not reproducible as published (tier C, not A). Serialize benchmarks time construction of the test object inside the loop for both Thrift and Protobuf (createThriftTestData / createProtobufTestData are called in every iteration), so the ratios mix object population with encoding; deserialize runs exclude the serialize step via BenchmarkSuspender. Protobuf rows copy into an IOBuf (SerializeToArray, SerializeAsString plus copyBuffer, ZeroCopy stream), a choice that may favour Thrift. One tiny synthetic schema, no strings of realistic length. fbthrift is described by the project list as Facebook's branch of Apache Thrift; is_fork_of left null because the upstream URL was not opened and cpp2 is largely independent code. Ratios are derived from the time/iter column; the file also lists a relative-percent column that agrees.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: seed-record pass starting from https://github.com/facebook/fbthrift; README only says 'fast serialization', so the repo tree was searched and thrift/lib/cpp2/protocol/benchmark/ (ProtobufTestData.proto, ThriftProtocolBenchmarks.cpp) was opened

name: CRoaring (Roaring Bitmaps)
baseline: uncompressed bitset with the same word-array representation as std::bitset/std::vector<bool> (the paper's own portable C reimplementation, 'cbitset', is used in the benchmark rather than literally std::bitset or std::vector<bool>)
workload: 8 realistic integer-set datasets (CensusInc, CensusInc-sorted, Census1881, Census1881-sorted, Weather, Weather-sorted, Wikileaks, Wikileaks-sorted; 200 sets each, universe sizes 200K-4.3M): sequential iteration/cardinality, random-access membership queries at n/4, n/2, 3n/4, and 199 pairwise intersections/unions/differences/symmetric differences between successive sets. Reported as CPU cycles per input value.
claimed_speedup: Mixed by dataset and operation. Intersections (Table 7a, cycles/value): bitset 19.5 vs Roaring 0.090 on Census1881 (~217x faster, derived from page data); bitset 33.0 vs Roaring 0.140 on Census1881-sorted (~236x, derived from page data); bitset 26.4 vs Roaring 1.43 on Wikileaks (~18x, derived from page data). But on CensusInc/CensusInc-sorted/Weather, the plain bitset is FASTER than Roaring (e.g. bitset 0.130 vs Roaring 0.220-0.380 cycles/value on CensusInc, i.e. bitset ~1.7-2.9x faster there). Random-access membership queries (Table 6): plain bitset wins on every dataset (2.4-3.7 cycles vs Roaring's 17-77 cycles). Memory (Table 4): Roaring uses far less than an uncompressed bitset on sparse data, e.g. 2.60 vs 524 bits/value on Census1881, 0.34 vs 11.4 bits/value on Weather-sorted.
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 5.4, compiled with -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake, 3.4 GHz, 32KB L1d, 256KB L2/core, 8MB L3), 32GB DDR4-2133 dual-channel, single-threaded, Turbo Boost disabled, timed with rdtsc, results reproducible within 5%
stars_or_usage: 1,887 stars; used by Apache Doris, ClickHouse, Alibaba Tair, Redpanda, YDB, StarRocks
tradeoffs: Roaring wins decisively on memory and on set-algebra over sparse/clustered 32-bit integer sets, but loses to a plain uncompressed bitset on random-access membership queries (bitset has roughly an order of magnitude lower latency) and can lose on set-algebra for dense/small-universe datasets. Targets dynamic sparse 32-bit integer sets, not fixed-size dense bit flags, so it is not a general drop-in for std::bitset<N> or std::vector<bool>.
caveats: The paper's 'bitset' baseline is the authors' own portable C library ('cbitset', github.com/lemire/cbitset: ceil(n/64) 64-bit words, no processor-specific optimizations), not literally std::bitset or std::vector<bool> from a standard library implementation, though it is representationally identical to both, so baseline_in_list is recorded true with reduced confidence. Results are strongly dataset- and operation-dependent; the entry reports both wins and losses rather than a single headline number. Authors of the paper are also the library's maintainers (Lemire et al., published in Software: Practice and Experience, 2018), but code, compiler, flags, and CPU model are all public and stated, satisfying Tier A methodology regardless of who ran it.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'CRoaring roaring bitmap benchmark std::bitset std::vector<bool>' -> https://github.com/RoaringBitmap/CRoaring; benchmark tables opened via https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.07821 (Lemire, Kaser, Kurz, Deri, O'Hara, Saint-Jacques, Ssi-Yan-Kai)

name: plf::bitset (plf_bitsets)
workload: Full bitset test-suite exercised in a loop (set/reset/shift/index/etc.); separately, set_range/reset_range on a 128000-bit bitset over 10000 randomly chosen ranges per run.
claimed_speedup: Release (O2, AVX2): 24% (GCC)/20% (MSVC) faster overall test suite; 34,652%/67,612% faster set_range/reset_range; ~101%/98% faster left/right shift (GCC), 35%/22% (MSVC); 6%/204% faster set(pos,val); 3%/0% faster operator[]. Debug builds show much larger gaps (up to 428,127%/750,726% for set_range/reset_range).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2 (nuwen mingw) and MSVC 2022; release build: O2, AVX2, C++23
hardware: Intel i7-9750H, Windows 10 (safe mode)
tradeoffs: plf::bitset omits std::bitset's from-string/from-ulong constructors; adds set_range/reset_range, range-based any/all/none/count, an allocation-free XOR swap, index-bounds-checking via a template flag, and a user-supplied-buffer variant (plf::bitsetb) not present in std::bitset.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project author's own numbers), not independently reproduced, though methodology (compiler, flags, hardware) and full benchmark source are published. The extreme set_range/reset_range percentages (up to ~677x) largely reflect that std::bitset has no native ranged-set primitive (callers must loop bit-by-bit), so this is partly an algorithmic-complexity win (O(1) words vs O(n) bits) rather than a raw constant-factor speedup; the overall test-suite numbers (~20-24%) are the more representative figure for general use. Licensed under 'Computing For Good License v1.01' (zlib-like but with additional ethical-use-restriction clauses 4a-4e), which is not OSI-approved due to those field-of-use restrictions, so usability is 'reference' rather than 'copyable'.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'bitset faster than std::bitset benchmark github' -> https://github.com/mattreecebentley/plf_bitsets; full methodology at https://plflib.org/bitsets.htm

name: pasta::bit_vector
baseline: cs-poppy (Zhou, Andersen & Kaminsky, SEA'13 compact rank/select bit-vector structure)
workload: rank and select queries on a length-n uncompressed bit vector, at ~3.51% space overhead
claimed_speedup: up to 8% faster rank and up to 16.5% faster select vs cs-poppy, at equal space overhead
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20; GPL-3.0 is more restrictive than MIT/BSD peers; adds rank/select operations that std::bitset/std::vector<bool> lack entirely, so it's an additive capability rather than a drop-in replacement; fastest variant relies on SIMD and -march=native.
caveats: std::bitset/std::vector<bool> have no native rank/select, so there is no direct std baseline for this functionality; the recorded baseline (cs-poppy) is the field's standard compact rank/select structure (Zhou et al., SEA'13), not a mainstream stdlib facility, which is why baseline_in_list=false and confidence is capped. This is a peer-reviewed paper (Kurpicz, SPIRE 2022) with public benchmark code (github.com/pasta-toolbox/bit_vector_experiments), but the exact compiler flags and CPU model used for the paper's reported numbers were not confirmed on the pages opened this session (only generic CMake build presets were found in the repo README), so it is scored B rather than A.
found_via: GitHub: `gh search repos "succinct data structure" --language c++ --sort stars` -> pasta-toolbox/bit_vector; claim verified against paper abstract at arxiv.org/abs/2206.01149

name: better_bitset
workload: Find index of first set bit ('first_one') across bitsets of size 4-8192 bits, ~5 average one-bits per bitset, 1000 random bitsets per size, measured with Google Benchmark; the std::bitset side is a manual bit-by-bit loop using .test(i), since std::bitset has no built-in bit-scan for sizes above 64.
claimed_speedup: README claims 'improvements averaging 60x' versus the iterative std::bitset approach. benchmark/results.txt shows e.g. N=8192: 953,294 ns (std::bitset loop) vs 18,134 ns (better_bitset) = ~52.6x faster (derived from page data); N=64: 6,349 ns vs 213 ns = ~29.8x faster (derived from page data); N=8: 701 ns vs 218 ns = ~3.2x faster (derived from page data).
hardware: 20 logical CPUs @ ~3609.6 MHz (Google Benchmark auto-detected clock speed and cache sizes only; exact CPU model name not recorded)
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement: only implements first_zero/first_one plus the common subset (all/any/none/count/size/set/reset/flip/to_string); lacks bitwise operators and the std::bitset reference-proxy type. Also smaller than std::bitset for sizes <=16 bits.
caveats: Small, unmaintained (last commit 2022, 8 stars) repo. Benchmark is first-party and its results.txt (Google Benchmark output) records no compiler name or optimization flags, and identifies the CPU only by core count/clock speed rather than model, so it falls short of Tier A methodology despite having public benchmark code and real numbers. No LICENSE file in the repo, so the code can be studied but not safely reused.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch '"Bitset2" ClaasBontus header-only bitset benchmark std::bitset' surfaced https://github.com/MrElectrify/better_bitset; benchmark folder and results opened at github.com/MrElectrify/better_bitset/tree/master/benchmark

name: BitLib
workload: Google Benchmark micro-benchmarks of STL-style algorithms (set, shift_left/right, reverse, transform (unary/binary), rotate, count, swap_ranges, copy, equal, move, copy_backward, fill, find) over bit containers of size 2^8 (small) through 2^31 (huge) bits, run against bit::bit_vector, pinam45/dynamic_bitset, noporpoise/BitArray, and std::vector<bool>.
claimed_speedup: bit::shift_left ~283x faster than std::shift_left at large size (371,224 ns vs 105,227,752 ns, derived from page data); bit::reverse ~236x faster at large size (1,245,260 ns vs 293,563,397 ns, derived); bit::count ~161x faster at large size (365,194 ns vs 58,934,071 ns, derived); bit::rotate ~70x faster at large size (7,333,284 ns vs 514,697,313 ns, derived); bit::set ~1.26x faster at large size (1.90 ns vs 2.39 ns, derived)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++17+; bit_vector wraps std::vector<WordType> and mirrors std::vector<bool>'s interface, but the speedups only apply when using BitLib's own bit::-namespaced algorithms (bit::rotate, bit::transform, etc.) instead of <algorithm>; optional SIMD path requires opting into Google Highway (BITLIB_HWY).
caveats: This is the assignment's known lead. The README's benchmark table has no stated compiler flags or CPU model, so tier is capped at C even though the benchmark code (Google Benchmark, BITLIB_BENCHMARK CMake option) is public. Several ratios exceed 50x (shift_left, reverse, transform at 'large' sizes), which is plausible given std::vector<bool>'s well-documented bit-by-bit iteration cost in libstdc++/libc++, but cannot be independently verified without stated methodology. 11 open issues; last commit 2024-06-06 (stale).
found_via: GitHub: assignment's known lead (bkille/BitLib); confirmed via `gh api repos/bkille/BitLib` and its README "Performance Benchmarks" section

name: sul::dynamic_bitset
workload: Same third-party Google Benchmark suite as BitLib (shift_left/right, transform, count, fill) at 'small' (256-bit) and 'large' (16,777,216-bit) sizes, comparing sul::dynamic_bitset against std::vector<bool>.

No compiler flags or CPU model stated anywhere in the source; several ratios exceed 50x, so tier is capped at C per the implausible-ratio rule.

name: sdsl::bit_vector (SDSL - Succinct Data Structure Library)
claimed_speedup: Project's own description (SDSL 3.0 docs/wiki): sdsl::bit_vector is 'an optimized replacement of the infamous std::vector<bool>'. No numeric benchmark located for this specific claim within the research budget.
stars_or_usage: 2,309 stars; de facto standard succinct-data-structures library, extremely widely cited in the IR/bioinformatics/text-indexing literature (e.g. underlies the SPIRE 2014 sdsl-lite paper and dozens of downstream tools)
tradeoffs: bit_vector itself is a packed bit array similar in spirit to std::vector<bool> but without a standard-library iterator/allocator interface or thread-safety guarantees for concurrent bit writes; the library's real value is the rank/select/compressed layers built on top (rrr_vector, sd_vector, wt_*), which are not literal std::vector<bool>/std::bitset drop-ins and add their own space/time tradeoffs.
caveats: Could not confirm a specific numeric benchmark for bit_vector vs std::vector<bool> within the tool budget for this run; the 'optimized replacement' framing is a first-party claim with no accompanying numbers found, so this is Tier D. Included as this run's one allowed Tier-D entry because the project is unambiguously notable (2.3k stars, foundational in its field). Repository has not been pushed to since 2023-06-02 (>3 years), so maintenance_status is 'abandoned' despite the project's continued heavy citation/usage.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'succinct rank select bit vector github faster than std::vector<bool> C++' -> https://github.com/simongog/sdsl-lite

name: Armadillo
baseline: IT++ and Newmat (C++ matrix libraries; no BLAS-vs-Armadillo number on the page)
workload: Timed loops of small and medium dense-matrix expressions (A+B, A+B+C+D, A*B*C*D chains, row copy into a submatrix, trans(p)*inv(diagmat(q))*r), 4x4 to 1000x800 doubles, N chosen so each test runs at least 5 seconds.
claimed_speedup: Approximate speed-ups over IT++/Newmat: add two matrices 4x4 15x/10x, 100x100 3.5x/same speed; add four matrices 100x100 6x/1.5x; multiply four matrices (100x80..40x20) 2.5x/10x and (1000x800..400x200) 2.5x/20x; submatrix row copy 4x4 16x/44x, 100x100 2x/4.5x; multi-operation expression 4x4 77x/23x, 100x100 1086x/5x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.3.0 (optimisation flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core2 Duo CPU (2 GHz, 2 MB cache), Linux kernel 2.6.26
tradeoffs: Header-only template library with delayed evaluation (expression templates); big decompositions and large matrix products still call out to LAPACK/BLAS (OpenBLAS, MKL), so large-matrix speed depends on the linked BLAS rather than on Armadillo itself.
caveats: First-party numbers from a Core2 Duo / Linux 2.6.26 / GCC 4.3.0 setup (an old machine and compiler); compiler flags and exact CPU model are not stated, only a code extract (not the full harness) is shown, and results are shown as graphs with 'approximate speed-up' labels. The baselines are two older, less-used C++ matrix libraries (IT++, Newmat), not BLAS or Eigen, so the guessed BLAS baseline is not what was beaten; the big wins come from avoiding temporaries in small or chained expressions (1086x case is a single-loop fusion), not from faster kernels. name: atomic_queue
workload: SPSC round-trip ping-pong: 2 threads exchange a 4-byte int counter 1,000,000 times via two queue instances (lowest-contention case); also an N-producer/N-consumer throughput scalability test moving 1,000,000 messages through one queue, run across AMD Ryzen 5950X, Ryzen 5825U, Intel i9-9900KS and Intel Xeon Gold 6132.
claimed_speedup: AtomicQueue mean round-trip latency 42ns vs std::mutex 320ns on Ryzen 5950X (~7.6x lower); OptimistAtomicQueue 33ns (~9.7x lower). At 1-producer/1-consumer throughput: AtomicQueue 142.7M msg/s vs std::mutex 4.1M msg/s (~34x); OptimistAtomicQueue reports up to ~1.23B msg/s in the same 1P/1C cell, which is an implausible outlier (see caveats).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0 (primary systems; gcc-8.4.0 on legacy i9-9900KS/Xeon Gold systems); Makefile release flags: -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -std=c++14 -falign-functions=64 -DNDEBUG
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X and Ryzen 5825U (KDE Neon/Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, mitigations=off); legacy: Intel i9-9900KS (Kubuntu 18.04) and Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (RHEL 6.10)
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Fixed capacity set at compile/construction time (ring buffer, no heap growth); no OS-blocking wait, only busy-spin (push/pop can't sleep, unsuitable for non-latency-critical code that wants to yield the CPU); atomic-element variants reserve a NIL sentinel value that must never be pushed; value-semantics only (copies/moves elements, no in-place references).
caveats: The 1P/1C throughput cell for OptimistAtomicQueue (~1.23B msg/s, stdev ~135M) is far above what its own 42/33ns latency numbers would imply and is almost certainly a measurement/compiler-hoisting artifact of the fully uncontended, dependency-free loop rather than a sustained rate; treat the 7.6-9.7x latency figures as the solid claim and discount the >200x throughput figure. Throughput scaling is also non-monotonic across some thread counts (e.g. std::mutex briefly outperforms AtomicQueue at exactly 2 threads on the 5950X), which the author's own charts show and do not hide.

name: Wirehair
baseline: CM256 (catid/cm256, O(N^2) Cauchy-matrix MDS Reed-Solomon codec; Longhair measured alongside)
workload: Erasure-code encode and decode throughput for 128 data pieces of 64,000 bytes with 128 recovery pieces (code rate 1/2), WH256 (Wirehair with the GF256 inner loops) vs CM256, Longhair, FEC-AL and Leopard, on the author's AVX2 laptop.
claimed_speedup: Leopard's Benchmarks.md: WH256 wirehair_encode(N = 128) 661.644 MB/s and wirehair_decode 830.103 MB/s vs CM256 encode 99.6658 MBps and decode 104.651 MBps (Longhair 100.342 and 96.3757 MB/s), i.e. about 6.6x faster encode and 7.9x faster decode than CM256 (derived from page data). Text: Wirehair 'Encodes at 660 MB/s, and decodes at 830 MB/s for ALL cases' and is the fastest decoder in that comparison; Wirehair's README also states it scales as O(N) rather than O(N log N) (Leopard) or O(N^2) (Fecal).
hardware: Author's 'few year old' laptop with AVX2 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Not an MDS code: needs N + 0.02 packets on average and sometimes N + 1 or N + 2 (Benchmarks.md says about a 3% chance of one extra block). Rateless fountain code for large block counts (up to 64,000). Same page shows Leopard encodes about 3x faster (1.96 GB/s) at k=m=128, and the Fecal README shows FEC-AL encoding about 2x faster than Wirehair at N=1000 with about 100 losses and 4x faster with about 30 losses (Wirehair decodes about 2x faster at 100 losses, but 2x slower at 30). The Wirehair README itself calls it a pretty inefficient codec for N below about 128 compared with Fecal. Public C API; versioned wire profiles in the current tree.
caveats: First-party numbers from the same author as CM256, 'not being very rigorous' on one laptop, with no CPU model, compiler or flags, and one configuration (k=m=128, 64 KB pieces). The measured code is catid/wh256, a pre-production GF256 branch, not necessarily the current catid/wirehair tree. The numbers sit in the Leopard repo, not Wirehair's. Reed-Solomon (MDS, practical only up to 255 pieces) and a fountain code are not like-for-like. Baseline is the author's own CM256 rather than Jerasure, ISA-L or Zfec, and the author notes CM256's inner loops could still be improved with GF256. Wirehair's own README benchmarks only compare Wirehair 1 with Wirehair 2 (GCC 13.3, Threadripper PRO 9985WX) and show WH2 slower at 64-byte blocks, so they are no evidence against an outside baseline. Category erasure-codes is not one of the wave categories; filed under compression-and-encoding as the nearest domain.

name: pixz
workload: Compress and decompress a 3 GB CSV file (about 17 million tweets) through the R package pRDS's command-line wrappers at default levels (xz = 6), on a 4-core, 8-thread i7 Mac.
claimed_speedup: pRDS README benchmark table: pixz write 443 s, read 63 s, size 805 MB versus xz write 469 s, read 64 s, size 795 MB (pixz about 1.06x faster to compress and about 1.02x faster to decompress, derived from page data; output 1.3% larger, derived). Other rows: 7z 580 s write, 83 s read, 741 MB; R native xz 2626 s write, 105 s read, 772 MB (pixz about 5.9x faster than R's built-in xz, derived from page data). The pixz README itself gives no numbers, only the claims that pixz parallelizes decompression and defaults to all cores while xz defaults to one.
hardware: i7 Mac, 4 cores / 8 threads (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Splits input into independent xz blocks (loses some compression ratio versus one large block, 805 MB versus 795 MB in the table above), adds a tarball index for fast listing and single-file extraction, output is a normal .xz stream with an added index; needs libarchive and liblzma; flags differ from xz (-z, -c, -f, -l, -q, -t mean different things).
caveats: Weak evidence: one loosely controlled run by a third party (the pRDS author says 'not in an entirely scientific manner', 'loosely controlled environment', and that four tools did not work as intended on the machine), no tool versions, no flags, no CPU model, no repeat runs. The 'xz' row is not stated to be single-threaded or multi-threaded (the 469 s figure is plausible for single-threaded xz -6 on 3 GB), and a 6% gain from 8 threads suggests pixz was not parallelizing well in that setup. Modern xz (5.2 and later) has its own -T threading, so the pixz README's 'xz defaults to one core' framing is now only a default difference. The pixz repo has no benchmark of its own and the README makes no speed numbers. Directional only; filed to record that no stronger public pixz-versus-xz measurement was reachable (pxz and pigz benchmark pages found by search were not pixz-specific, and the neurolabusc/pigz-bench README does not cover xz or pixz).

name: TurboRLE (TRLE and SRLE)
baseline: rle8 (rainerzufalldererste/rle8, SSE/AVX2 8-bit run length encoder) and Mespotine RLE (MRLE); memcpy shown as a reference row
workload: Single-thread run length encode and decode throughput (MB/s) and compressed size on three large files: girl.bmp (RLE64Samples), a checkers end-game tablebase file (1034.db), and enwik9 after a Burrows-Wheeler transform (enwik9bwt), measured with TurboBench.
claimed_speedup: README claim: 'Compress better and up to 12 times faster and decompress up to 6 times faster than other fast RLEs'; 'Can be faster than memcpy!'. Skylake table (MB/s, C = compress, D = decompress): girl.bmp trle C 2089 / D 11385, srle 8 C 11307 / D 13205 (4744806 bytes) vs rle8 C 890 / D 11998 (5901235 bytes) and mrle C 378 / D 12302; enwik9bwt trle C 472 / D 1743, srle 8 C 568 / D 4310 vs rle8 C 260 / D 675 and mrle C 207 / D 553; 1034.db trle C 774 / D 3020 vs rle8 C 456 / D 2669 and mrle C 262 / D 1491. Derived from page data: srle 8 compresses girl.bmp about 12.7x faster than rle8 and decompresses enwik9bwt about 6.4x faster than rle8; trle compresses girl.bmp about 2.3x faster than rle8 while decompressing slightly slower (11385 vs 11998 MB/s). srle 64 compresses girl.bmp at 16269 MB/s vs memcpy 13978 MB/s (output is larger, 19839711 bytes).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.3 (tables dated 2019-08); flags not stated in the README. The current TurboBench makefile builds the TurboRLE objects with -O3 -march=haswell -w -fstrict-aliasing -falign-loops=32 -DNDEBUG on x86_64, but that is the HEAD makefile, not the 2019 revision, and the rle8 baseline object flags are not shown the same way.
hardware: Intel Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz (x86 tables); ARM A73 ODROID-N2 1.8GHz (second set of tables, same ordering)
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0-or-later (copyleft; a commercial licence is not described in the README). Pure C with no inline assembly, SIMD paths for SSE/AVX2/NEON plus a RISC-V scalar fallback, and Java JNI bindings. Several variants (srle 8/16/32/64) trade compression ratio for speed, so the fastest rows compress much worse than rle8 or mrle: the 12x and 6x figures pair different output sizes.
caveats: Tier C because the benchmark tables are first-party, dated 2019-08, with the compiler version and CPU stated but no flags in the README (TurboBench is public, so a verifier may be able to raise this to A by reproducing from the makefile). The baselines are other RLE libraries, not a stdlib facility; 'up to' numbers cherry-pick the best variant per file (srle 8 vs rle8 on girl.bmp; srle 8 decompress vs rle8 on enwik9bwt). TurboRLE trle is slower than rle8 and mrle at decompression on girl.bmp (11385 vs 11998 and 12302 MB/s), so the 'decompress faster' claim does not hold on every file. The README table rows for rle8 and mrle show only one rle8 configuration (rle8 1). The memcpy row and the 'faster than memcpy' claim apply only to compression of highly compressible data.

baseline: Boost Graph Library (Boost.Graph 1.84.0, via the perf/boost benchmarks for Dijkstra, BFS, Kruskal, Prim, greedy and Welsh-Powell colouring)

Pull-request numbers (web_google / web_berkstan, Graaf time relative to Boost) after the September 2026 vector-storage optimisations: Kruskal 1.14x / 1.60x slower (PR #451, was 3.48x / 3.20x); Prim 2.01x / 1.85x slower (PR #452); greedy colouring 2.13x / 7.70x slower (PR #455); Welsh-Powell 2.59x / 5.71x slower (PR #456); BFS 3.55x / 8.65x slower (PR #449); Dijkstra single path 4.38x / 12.56x slower (PR #453, still open when read); dijkstra_shortest_paths 6.94x / 17.01x slower (PR #454). name: klib khash (khash.h)
workload: udb2 micro-benchmark: count occurrences of N 32-bit integer keys (about 25% distinct) in a uint32-to-uint32 hash map, with identity hash for both tables, six rounds with N = 10M, 18M, 26M, 34M, 42M, 50M, so rehashing growth is included; reports CPU time and peak-RSS delta.
claimed_speedup: At N=50M (180929 server log): khash 5.460 s and 172.457 MB versus std::unordered_map 22.220 s and 493.762 MB, about 4.1x less CPU time and 2.9x less memory (derived from log data); at N=10M 0.652 s versus 2.972 s (4.6x, derived). Second variant (run-test-1, emplace-based for std::unordered_map): 4.724 s / 136.742 MB versus 22.872 s / 493.363 MB at N=50M (4.8x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 5.4.0 per udb2 README for the server run; khash/Makefile builds with 'cc -O2 -Wall', c++11/Makefile builds std::unordered_map with 'c++ -O3 -Wall -std=c++11' (so the baseline got the higher optimization level). libstdc++ is inferred from gcc on Linux, not stated.
hardware: Linux server, Xeon E5-2683 v3 2.0GHz, 35MB cache, 640GB memory (udb2 README)
tradeoffs: Single-header C macro library (KHASH_INIT instantiates types and functions per key/value type), so no templates, RAII, or iterator stability; open addressing with 32-bit bucket indices (khint_t), values stored in a separate array and relocated on resize; deletion leaves tombstones. Pointers or references into the table are invalidated by insertion. Keys and values must be trivially copyable plain types; custom types need hand-written hash and equality macros. The klib README also advertises kbtree.h (B-tree ordered map), ksort.h, and kvec.h, but no numeric comparison against std::map, std::sort, or std::vector was reachable here (their blog posts are on blocked wordpress).
caveats: The benchmark lives in a separate repo (attractivechaos/udb2, same author) and the numbers are inside the linked tgz (khash/run-test.log and c++11/run-test.log); the udb2 README itself shows only plots. The 180929 run is from 2018 with gcc 5.4.0 and an old libstdc++ (unordered_map design has not changed since). Only 32-bit integer keys and values with an identity hash, counting workload; says nothing about string keys, deletions heavy loads (run-test-del variants exist but were not read), or lookup-only loads. The README's 'plots vary with machines' warning applies: the Google Cloud n1-standard-1 run uses different hardware. CPU time (getrusage user+sys), single run per N. The same repo also lists many other maps (absl, ska, tsl, robin_hood, unordered_dense, verstable, and others), so khash is only one of several that can be compared with std::unordered_map; their rows were not read. The udb2 repo has no stated license in the page content.

name: M*LIB (m-dict hash map, DICT_DEF2)
baseline: std::unordered_map (GNU libstdc++ STL; also std::vector, std::set, std::string in the same suite)
workload: c-stl-comparison bench: UMap U64 inserts 20,000,000 random unsigned long key/value pairs then performs 20,000,000 random lookups (about half found); the same harness also times a string-key map, a 256-byte-key map, a growing array, a sorted set and string replace. Time is best of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: EPYC 7763 run on the repo's result branch: UMap U64 M*LIB dict 923.10 ms vs STL unordered_map 11670.18 ms (12.6x, derived from page data), dict Bulk 737.57 ms (15.8x, derived), open-addressing dict 934.82 ms; UMap Str dict 815.71 ms vs STL umap 2930.79 ms (3.6x, derived); UMap Big dict 1139.77 ms vs STL umap 4185.96 ms (3.7x, derived); Seq(Array) 690.71 ms vs STL vector 1560.62 ms (2.3x, derived); SSet B+tree 813.29 ms vs STL Rbtree 2627.84 ms (3.2x, derived); String Replace 536.51 ms vs STL 1396.06 ms (2.6x, derived). Memory for UMap U64 dict 589.90M vs STL umap 933.78M. README says 'M*LIB is on par with the STL or even faster' (graphs only, GNU C++ STL v10.2).
compiler_and_flags: bench/Makefile: CFLAGS=-O2 -march=native, C built with cc -std=c11, STL side built with c++ -std=c++11 (g++, so libstdc++), each bench run with --quiet --best --repeat 3. GCC version is not in BENCH.md; the project wiki page Benchmark-result states GCC 16.1 with -O2 -march=native; the M*LIB README graphs state GNU C++ STL v10.2.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, lscpu line in BENCH.md); an i5-3210M result is also published in the repo (master branch bench/doc/BENCH.md).
tradeoffs: Pure C99/C11 header-only library that generates typed containers with preprocessor macros (oplists); explicit init/clear calls, no copy by assignment, container hands out borrowed pointers; default policy aborts the program on allocation failure (customisable); no C++ templates, exceptions or iterators in the STL sense. Sorted-set variants include a B+tree that is not API-equivalent to std::set.
caveats: Benchmark harness is the library author's own repo (P-p-H-d/c-stl-comparison), run on a shared GitHub-hosted CI VM, so timings are noisy and no CPU pinning is stated; GCC version is not printed in BENCH.md. STL rows use default std::hash (identity for integers), no reserve() and operator[] inserts, so the 12.6x U64 gap is partly default-std::unordered_map node-allocation cost, and other open-addressing C++ maps would narrow it (Boost unordered flat map is 1464.12 ms on the same page, 7.97x faster than STL; KLIB khash 1257.84 ms). M*LIB is not uniformly faster: in the same BENCH.md STL Sort is 1105.64 ms vs M*LIB Sort 1706.60 ms (STL 1.54x faster; stable sort 1237.25 vs 1285.71 ms, close) and STL SSet(Rbtree) 2627.84 ms beats M*LIB SSet(Rbtree) 3092.66 ms (the win is the B+tree). Seq(Deque) 896.94 vs 1799.15 ms and Seq(List) 971.39 vs 1193.67 ms are smaller wins. Ratios are derived from page data, not stated by the project. The M*LIB README Performance section shows only PNG graphs against GNU C++ STL v10.2, so the table above is the checkable evidence. The mlib commit pinned in BENCH.md (4acdfe4) is the current master head.

caveats: Compiler optimization flags not explicitly stated alongside the compiler version; only one hardware configuration tested.
found_via: WebSearch: 'rigtorp HashMap open addressing benchmark std::unordered_map'; opened https://github.com/rigtorp/HashMap README benchmark section directly

name: SIGMOD 2025 Contest Solution - Hash Join Pipeline (Robin Hood/Hopscotch/Cuckoo/Unchained)
workload: Hash-join pipeline over the IMDB dataset (SIGMOD 2025 Programming Contest query set), comparing a std::unordered_map-based join baseline against custom open-addressing hash tables (Robin Hood, Hopscotch, Cuckoo) and then a custom 'Unchained' hashtable with columnar late-materialization and parallel build/probe.
claimed_speedup: Baseline (std::unordered_map): ~112s total runtime. Part 1 (custom Robin Hood/Hopscotch/Cuckoo hash tables): ~108s, ~3% faster. Part 2 (Unchained hashtable + column-store/late materialization): ~16s, ~86% reduction vs Part 1. Part 3 (parallel build/probe + slab allocator): ~7s, ~56% reduction vs Part 2. Final: 'Final speedup: ~16x faster than baseline'.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 18, CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (repo built/run on macOS)
hardware: MacBook Pro, Apple M4 Pro (14 cores), 48GB RAM
tradeoffs: This is a full application pipeline built for one contest workload (column-store, late materialization, custom slab allocator, work-stealing parallel probe), not a drop-in std::unordered_map replacement library -- the individual header files (RobinHoodHash.hpp, HopscotchHash.hpp, CuckooHash.hpp, Unchained.hpp) could be extracted, but only ~3% of the eventual 16x came from swapping the hash table itself; the rest came from column-store layout and parallelism. Single dataset (IMDB) benchmark.
caveats: Coursework project (University of Athens K23a course) by three students, 1 GitHub star, no independent replication. Reporting '16x faster than std::unordered_map' without noting that most of the gain is architectural (not the hash table swap) overstates the hash table's own contribution. libc++ is inferred from the macOS/Clang toolchain, not stated explicitly in the repo.
found_via: gh search repos "hash map faster than std::unordered_map" --sort stars --limit 20

name: uthash
workload: Third-party C/C++ hash-table benchmark (uthash v2.3.0 vs std::unordered_map among 15 tables): tables grown to 20,000,000 keys at max load factor 0.875 with a shared MurmurHash3-finalizer/FNV-1a hash, measuring insert, erase and replace of existing keys, erase and lookup of existing and nonexisting keys, and iteration, for three key/value shapes (32-bit/32-bit, 64-bit/448-bit, 16-char string/64-bit).
claimed_speedup: Article text: "uthash's iteration is about twice as fast as std::unordered_map's iteration (albeit still extremely slow)". Heatmap for 0-20M keys (total time relative to the fastest table, std::unordered_map vs uthash): iterate 87.83 vs 37.39 (32-bit keys), 24.67 vs 10.53 (64-bit key/448-bit value), 79.94 vs 30.64 (string keys), i.e. 2.3-2.6x (derived from page data); erase existing 11.26 vs 7.79, 9.84 vs 6.10, 3.21 vs 2.41, i.e. 1.3-1.6x (derived from page data); erase nonexisting 5.25 vs 3.72, 5.83 vs 3.91, 2.43 vs 1.93, i.e. 1.3-1.5x (derived from page data); lookup nonexisting 3.67 vs 3.22, 3.96 vs 3.24, 2.32 vs 1.83, i.e. 1.1-1.3x (derived from page data); insert 64-bit/448-bit 4.91 vs 4.11 and string 2.87 vs 2.61 (1.1-1.2x, derived from page data). uthash is NOT faster for 32-bit-key insert (6.75 vs 6.39), 32-bit and 64-bit/448-bit replace (3.80 vs 2.71, 2.90 vs 2.34) or 32-bit lookup of existing keys (2.58 vs 2.28).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2.0 via MinGW-w64, C++20, -O3 -DNDEBUG (README build line: g++ -I. -std=c++20 -static -O3 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wpedantic main.cpp)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, frequency locked at 90%
tradeoffs: Macro-based intrusive hash table: every item embeds a 56-byte UT_hash_handle (per the benchmark article), node-based separate chaining like std::unordered_map, rudimentary API with the user writing much of the scaffolding. By default keys are hashed and compared byte-by-byte, which is unsafe for structs with padding bytes. Pure C, single header, BSD-1-Clause.
caveats: The numbers are a third-party comparison; uthash's own repo carries no benchmarks and never claims to beat std::unordered_map. The article's author concludes uthash 'should be avoided due to all-around poor performance' (it is far slower than open-addressing tables) and says its comments about std::unordered_map's poor performance also apply to uthash; the win over std::unordered_map is mixed. Heatmap figures are totals over the 0-20M-key run normalized to the fastest table, and the ratios here are derived from them. In the 0-200,000-key run (docs/result_2024-05-28T04_06_21.csv) uthash is slower than std::unordered_map for most insert, lookup and replace cases (for example 32-bit lookup of existing keys at N=200,000: 35,300 vs 15,700 in the CSV's time units, 2.25x slower, derived from CSV data), while at N=200,000 its iteration is faster only for the 64-bit/448-bit and string keys (derived from CSV data). Benchmarked version is uthash v2.3.0; the repo is now at v2.4.0. Run on Windows with MinGW-w64, so libstdc++ behaviour (including std::unordered_map growth policy) is specific to that build. The published article lives on github.io, which was blocked here; the numbers were read from the article source docs/index.md in the benchmark repo.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: seed record pass starting from http://troydhanson.github.io/uthash/ (listed in https://github.com/oz123/awesome-c#Data Structures); benchmark found via the JacksonAllan/c_cpp_hash_tables_benchmark README, which lists uthash v2.3.0 among its tables

name: Verstable
workload: Insertion, deletion, replacement, lookup, and iteration across three configurations: 32-bit int keys/values, 64-bit int keys with large values, and string keys.
claimed_speedup: Generally outperforms std::unordered_map (GCC's libstdc++) across the tested workloads, though it falls behind SIMD-based tables such as absl::flat_hash_map and boost::unordered_flat_map; exact ns/op figures are in the page's interactive charts, not extracted as text.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, 90% locked frequency
tradeoffs: C library (usable from C++ but not a drop-in std::unordered_map API); hybrid open-addressing/separate-chaining design with 4-bit hash fragments and tombstone-free deletion; behind absl/boost on raw speed.
caveats: Benchmark author is also Verstable's author (self-published, though methodology, compiler, and hardware are fully disclosed and the benchmark suite covers 15 tables including known independents like absl and boost).
found_via: WebSearch: 'hash table benchmark comparison std::unordered_map shootout' -> https://jacksonallan.github.io/c_cpp_hash_tables_benchmark/, then opened Verstable's README linking to this same benchmark

name: libcuckoo (cuckoohash_map, efficient/libcuckoo)
workload: Concurrent multi-threaded insert/lookup/mixed workloads on 120M 8-byte-key/8-byte-value pairs (Figure 1, 4-core, 1:1 read:write) and large-scale insert/lookup throughput on a 16-core machine
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed (EuroSys'14): on a 16-core machine the design executes 'almost 40 million inserts and more than 70 million lookup operations per second'; Figure 1 (4-core, 120M keys, 1:1 read/write) places it well above the C++11 std::unordered_map bar, though no exact std::unordered_map multiplier is printed as text (only 'up to 2.5x' vs Intel TBB concurrent_hash_map is quoted numerically)
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 (4-core Haswell) @ 3.4GHz, 32KB L1D / 256KB L2 / 8MB L3, 16GB DDR3 (main experiments); a separate 16-core machine is used for the headline ~40M insert/~70M lookup number
tradeoffs: Adds per-bucket spinlock/version-counter overhead irrelevant for single-threaded use; find() returns via out-parameter rather than iterator; requires locked_table() for safe bulk iteration; mainly wins when there is real concurrent contention, not necessarily in single-threaded use
caveats: The repo's current universal-benchmark harness (tests/universal-benchmark) only wires up LIBCUCKOO as a table type, no std::unordered_map baseline is compiled in; the concrete std::unordered_map comparison instead comes from the EuroSys 2014 paper's Figures 1-2, where the exact multiplier is visual (bar chart) rather than stated as text; the paper's one explicit numeric speedup ('up to 2.5x') is versus Intel TBB, not std::unordered_map
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "libcuckoo benchmark std::unordered_map throughput NSDI MemC3 concurrent hash table speedup"

name: sparsepp (spp::sparse_hash_map, greg7mdp/sparsepp)
workload: std::pair<uint64_t,uint64_t> entries inserted in random order into an initially empty, non-preallocated container; random insert, random lookup (known-present hits plus a 10%-present-probability miss set), and delete, up to ~70-100M entries
claimed_speedup: Author's write-up (bench.md): random insert throughput is 'as fast as the two std::unordered_map implementations' (g++ and Boost); random lookup is 'faster than all other alternatives, except for dense_hash_map'; delete is 'outperformed only by dense_hash_map' -- i.e. faster than std::unordered_map on lookup and delete, parity on insert
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.8.4 and Boost 1.55 (for the boost::unordered_map comparison line); optimization flags not explicitly stated
hardware: VirtualBox VM, 5.8GB total RAM / 5.7GB free before benchmarks, Ubuntu (~14.04)
tradeoffs: Slower than google::dense_hash_map on all three operations tested; the author's README now recommends greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap (or gtl) over sparsepp for C++11+ compilers; sparsepp is optimized for low peak memory during resize rather than raw speed
caveats: Results are presented as graph images in bench.md, not a text table, so exact numeric ratios could not be quoted verbatim; benchmark environment is an older VM from roughly 2016; the repo's own README steers users toward parallel-hashmap/gtl instead of sparsepp today
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "hash map faster than std::unordered_map benchmark github C++" (sparsepp/greg7mdp surfaced via related-library search)

name: tsl::ordered_map (Tessil/ordered-map)
workload: Insertion-order-preserving hash map/set benchmarked with the same Tessil shootout suite (int64 and string keys, insert/lookup/iteration)
claimed_speedup: README: 'O(1) average time complexity for lookups with performances similar to std::unordered_map but with faster insertions and reduced memory usage'; lookup speed is described as similar to, not faster than, std::unordered_map

name: tsl::robin_map (Tessil/robin-map)
workload: int64_t keys (identity hash), 15-char and 50-char std::string keys; insert, successful/unsuccessful lookup, and iteration across table sizes up to millions of elements
