name: CCAN htable (ccan/htable)
baseline: Judy arrays (JudyL, the Judy integer-key sparse array library)
workload: 50,000,000 objects, total time divided by object count to give ns per operation: initial insert, in-order (linear) hit and random hit lookups, with dense sequential keys and then with sparse keys after delete and reinsert; htable run at 75 percent full (dense), 37 percent full (sparse) and 37 percent full with pointer bit-stealing disabled (dumb).
claimed_speedup: htable wins random lookups and loses inserts and in-order lookups. Random hit, dense keys: Judy 361 ns, htable 330 (dense) / 357 (sparse) / 375 (dumb) ns. Random hit, sparse keys: Judy 736 ns, htable 405 / 386 / 445 ns, which is 1.65x to 1.9x faster (derived from page data). Judy wins initial insert (137 ns vs 332 / 471 / 482 ns) and linear hit (19 ns vs 174 / 176 / 214 ns on dense keys; 61 vs 215 / 202 / 265 ns on sparse keys).
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars (CCAN repo); search results show htable vendored in Samba (lib/ccan) and a 2014 htable licence-change request for Ruby
tradeoffs: Unordered hash table of pointers with user-supplied hash and equality callbacks (htable_type.h adds typed wrappers) and a pointer bit-stealing mode that saves memory; no ordered iteration, unlike Judy, which is sorted and wins on dense in-order access. LGPL-2.1+ licence, C only.
caveats: Snippet only: rusty.ozlabs.org was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the post was not opened; the numbers come from a web-search result summary of the post and could not be checked against the page, and the machine, CPU, compiler and flags are unknown (hence tier C and confidence 0.45). First-party author blog post from November 2010, on code that has been changed many times since (htable commits through August 2026). The repo's ccan/htable/tools/speed.c, stringspeed.c and hsearchspeed.c time htable alone (the only Judy reference is a comment about in-order lookups being cache-friendly for Judy), so the Judy comparison is not reproducible from the repo; no result numbers are published in the repo. Judy is a strong incumbent but not a standard-library facility, and the win is only on random-access lookups, not on inserts or sequential access. Searches of the CCAN _info files and tools found no other numeric comparison for any CCAN module.

name: Collections-C CC_HashTable (also CC_List, CC_Deque, CC_TreeTable)
baseline: std::unordered_map<int, void*> (also std::map, std::list, std::deque; the same run also compares GNOME glib 2.63.0 GHashTable/GTree/GList/GQueue and cdcontainers)
workload: Google Benchmark loops of N = 4 to 122,880 random-int operations on containers holding void* values: map insert, remove and search by key, iterator traversal; list push-front, push-back and insert-in-middle; deque push-front, push-back and insert at a random position. Each timed loop also calls a std::mt19937 random-number function per operation.
claimed_speedup: No ratios are written in the repo; it publishes SVG graphs only. Values read from the plotted points of those SVGs at N = 122,880 (derived from page data, approximate): CcHashTable vs std::unordered_map insert about 10.2 ms vs 49.4 ms (4.8x), remove 6.8 ms vs 24.9 ms (3.7x), search 8.1 ms vs 16.6 ms (2.0x), iterator traversal 2.2 ms vs 3.2 ms (1.5x); CcTreeTable vs std::map insert 44.5 ms vs 85.9 ms (1.9x), search 45.4 ms vs 84.3 ms (1.9x), traversal equal; CcList vs std::list push-back 5.1 ms vs 12.5 ms (2.4x), push-front 5.2 ms vs 12.3 ms (2.4x), insert-middle 5.8 ms vs 12.4 ms (2.2x); CcDeque vs std::deque push-back 4.6 ms vs 6.2 ms (1.3x), push-front 4.1 ms vs 6.2 ms (1.5x), random-position insert 337 ms vs 2560 ms (7.6x). CcTreeTable lookups are slower than std::unordered_map at large N (about 45 ms vs 17 ms for search), and glib's GHashTable beats CcHashTable on traversal and search.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler and version not stated. CMakeLists.txt defines Release flags '-O3 -flto -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti' (C: '-O3 -flto'), but run.sh calls plain 'cmake ..' with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so those flags apply only if the author passed Release by hand. Google Benchmark v1.5.0, glib 2.63.0, Collections-C pinned only to 'master' (late-2019 snapshot).
hardware: Quad-core Intel Core i7-7820HQ (3.9 GHz max), Linux 4.15.0-72-generic x86_64 (README 'Equipment' section)
tradeoffs: Generic containers store void* pointers (or sized variants), so there is no type safety and values need boxing or casting; the C library is LGPL-3.0 (library-linking terms apply). Insertion into CcHashTable and CcTreeTable needs a user hash and comparison function. Allocations use malloc per node like std::list and std::map.
caveats: Third-party but competing: the benchmark repo belongs to the author of the rival cdcontainers library, was last updated 2019-12-27, and its star count is not shown on the pages opened. Numbers exist only as matplotlib SVG graphs; the figures above were recovered from the SVG point positions. Compiler name and version are not stated and run.sh does not set a build type, so the optimisation level is unconfirmed (about 50 ns per std::deque push-back including the random call suggests an optimised build, but that is an inference). Every timed loop calls a mersenne-twister random function per operation, which dilutes the container difference for push-back/push-front. The std side stores int and the C side stores int cast to void*, with std::hash<int> as the C++ hash. Collections-C was built from an unpinned 'master' of December 2019 using the old unprefixed API (hashtable_add, deque_add_last); the library has since been renamed to the cc_ prefix, so the benchmark code does not match current master and the numbers predate later changes. No std::vector comparison exists. Tier capped at C because compiler and effective flags are unstated.

name: CYBHash
workload: Mapping Chinese futures/stock/option ticker symbols to values by converting the symbol string into an int64 key at runtime (borrowing ideas from qlibs/mph and MengRao/str) and then doing fast lookup, versus keying a std::unordered_map directly on the symbol.
claimed_speedup: README states 'approximately 10 times faster than std::unordered_map'; the repo's own GitHub description separately states 'approximately 5-30 times faster than std::unordered_map' -- the two first-party figures are inconsistent, and no benchmark script, raw numbers, or workload size is published.
tradeoffs: Only applicable to a narrow, domain-specific key space (Chinese futures/stock/option ticker symbols that can be packed into an int64); it is closer to a specialized key-encoding trick than a general-purpose hash map, and has no license, so the code cannot legally be reused/copied (study-only).
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (all-rights-reserved by default). Speedup claim is inconsistent between the README ('10x') and the repo description ('5-30x'). Zero benchmark methodology, hardware, compiler, or workload size disclosed anywhere in the repo, so the number cannot be independently checked.
found_via: gh search repos "hash map faster than std::unordered_map" --sort stars --limit 20

name: Grouped SIMD Hash Table
workload: Single-threaded insert+lookup benchmark with uint64 key/value pairs at up to 2M elements (~80% load factor), including a per-operation (insert / lookup-hit / lookup-miss) breakdown at 1M elements, using SSE2 grouped-metadata probing vs ankerl::unordered_dense's Robin Hood table.
claimed_speedup: At 1M elements: lookup-hit 1.69x faster, lookup-miss 1.21x faster, but insert 0.72x (i.e. ~1.4x slower) than ankerl::unordered_dense. Total wall time roughly ties/edges out ankerl at 1M (71.9ms vs 72.3ms) and 2M (156.3ms vs 157.4ms) elements; ankerl wins clearly at 100k-500k sizes.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -march=native -msse2 -std=c++17
tradeoffs: No deletion support, no resizing (fixed capacity, must be pre-sized), SSE2/x86-64 only (no ARM/NEON port), and the insert path is slower than the SOTA baseline it targets -- it only wins on lookup-heavy workloads above ~500k-1M elements.
caveats: Does NOT compare against std::unordered_map at all -- only against martinus/unordered_dense, which is itself already on the KNOWN_LIST as a faster-than-std project, so this is a comparison between two already-fast alternatives, not evidence against the stdlib baseline directly. Result is a narrow/mixed win (loses on inserts, roughly ties on total time). No CPU model stated, capping the tier below A. The README credits an AI 'Deep Research' tool and includes research-log files (INSIGHTS.md, EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md), suggesting an exploratory/automated project rather than a vetted, independently reviewed library; very new (~9 months) and low-adoption (50 stars).
found_via: gh search repos --topic hashmap --sort stars --limit 20, then gh search repos "hash table" "SIMD" --limit 20

name: parallel-hashmap (phmap)
workload: Inserting up to 100 million key/value pairs (two 8-byte integers) into phmap::flat_hash_map vs std::unordered_map, per the project's online design writeup.
claimed_speedup: "the Abseil flat_hash_map is significantly faster that the default stl implementation, typically about three times faster" (phmap::flat_hash_map is a header-only port of Abseil's swiss-table design); phmap::parallel_flat_hash_map is slightly slower than flat_hash_map for small tables, converging above ~80M values.
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 (exact optimization flags not stated)
tradeoffs: flat_hash_map/flat_hash_set move keys and values in memory, so pointers/iterators are invalidated on mutation, unlike std::unordered_map's node-based stability; node_hash_map avoids that at some speed/memory cost; the parallel_* variants add multithreading support and lower peak resize memory at the cost of being slightly slower for small tables. The author now steers new users to the C++20 successor repo 'gtl' (also by greg7mdp, not filed separately here since it shares the same design and no independent benchmark was found for it).
caveats: The '~3x faster' figure is stated on the project's own writeup page without a CPU model, exact compiler flags, or a linked raw-data/benchmark script for that specific number -- only the compiler (VS2017) is named, so this is capped at Tier C rather than A/B.
found_via: gh api repos/greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap (direct lookup); confirmed via https://greg7mdp.github.io/parallel-hashmap/

name: ska::flat_hash_map / ska::bytell_hash_map
workload: Successful/unsuccessful lookups, inserts (with/without reserve), erases, and mixed insert/erase sequences, on int and string keys with 4-, 32-, and 1024-byte values.
claimed_speedup: Author (Malte Skarupke) claims the fastest lookups of any hash table he tested, with inserts/erases also very fast, compared against std::unordered_map, boost::multi_index, and google::dense_hash_map in his 'I Wrote The Fastest Hashtable' post; exact numbers are shown only in the post's chart images, not as text.
tradeoffs: Robin Hood hashing with a log2(n) probe-count cap bounds worst-case lookup but adds complexity; default policy uses prime sizing (max load factor 0.5), power-of-two policy available as an alternative.
caveats: Compiler and hardware are not explicitly stated in the blog post (only 'Linux gcc' mentioned in passing); numbers are graph-only, no raw data table. Note: this is a different repo from skarupke/ska_sort, which is already on the known-list and excluded.

name: libsixel
workload: 100 sequential runs of the img2sixel command line (libsixel 1.10.5) encoding one 256x256 JPEG (Lenna) to Sixel, output to /dev/null, versus the same for chafa and sixrs.
claimed_speedup: img2sixel 1.10.5 1.64 s for 100 runs versus chafa 1.18.2 7.32 s (about 4.5x faster, derived from page data); sixrs 1.66 s (a tie with img2sixel). Output sizes: img2sixel 121,993 bytes, chafa 4,248,878 bytes, sixrs 59,220 bytes.

CPU model, libsixel and chafa build flags and the repo for the harness are not given, so this stays tier C. libsixel's own README, NEWS, ChangeLog and docs carry no benchmark numbers; the project emphasises quality and compatibility. libsixel's own site and the man pages were not opened.

name: SAIL

name: CPath
baseline: find (GNU findutils), TinyDir, Cute Files, Python os.walk
workload: Recursive vs. explicit-stack directory traversal over a large synthetic directory tree (C API and C++ bindings), averaged over 100 runs, measuring user/system/wall time, compared against `find`, Python os.walk, Cute Files, and TinyDir.
claimed_speedup: Wall time 0.082-0.083s for CPath (recursion/emplace, C and C++) vs 0.147s for `find`, 0.237s for Python os.walk, 0.284s for Cute Files, 0.294s for TinyDir -- roughly 1.8x faster than `find` and ~3.5x faster than TinyDir/Cute Files (project describes this as 'often around 3x faster than other libraries and even faster than find')
compiler_and_flags: -O3 (project states -O1/-O2 give the same result; -O0 is ~5% slower); compiler name not stated
hardware: MacBook Air7,2, Intel Core i5 @ 1.6GHz, 2 cores, 256KB L2 cache/core, 3MB L3, 8GB RAM
tradeoffs: C89/C99-era API by design for broad pre-C++17 compiler support; larger codebase (~2.5k lines) than minimal alternatives like TinyDir/Cute Files; does not eagerly load stat() info (opt-in), trading a feature for speed; author explicitly states CPath is 'NOT a replacement for a more heavy duty library like std::filesystem.'
caveats: The published benchmark compares against `find`, TinyDir, Cute Files, and Python os.walk -- not against std::filesystem directly -- and the README explicitly disclaims being a std::filesystem replacement, so this is reported as evidence against a related-but-different incumbent (baseline_in_list=false) with lower confidence for the stdlib-replacement framing. Benchmark is first-party and single-machine, and no compiler name is given.

name: mexce
baseline: native compiler-generated C++ code for the same expressions (statically compiled)
workload: Compile and evaluate a suite of 44,229 scalar math expressions at run time (SSE2 and x87 backends), average evaluation time per expression and total evaluation time, versus the same expressions compiled natively.
claimed_speedup: README table on GitHub Actions CI (Ubuntu runner): average evaluation 6.0 ns for the SSE2 backend versus 7.0 ns native (1.17x, derived from page data), total evaluation 27.2 ms versus 32.7 ms (1.20x, derived); SSE2 plus fast-math 6.0 ns and 26.8 ms; x87 backend 8.0 ns and 34.8 ms (slower than native); average compile time 174 us per expression for SSE2 and 135 us for x87. README: SSE2 'performs on par with or faster than native compiler-generated code'.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark target built Release with -O3 -DNDEBUG (GCC and Clang) or /O2 (MSVC) per CMakeLists.txt; the README table does not say which compiler produced the numbers
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu runner (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only; the SSE2 backend calls libm for transcendentals, the x87 backend uses 80-bit internal precision with more exact results; runtime compile cost of 135 to 177 microseconds per expression; executable memory (mmap or VirtualAlloc) required; fast-math option changes NaN and Inf semantics; optional protected-expression mode needs libsodium.
caveats: First-party numbers from a CI runner without a CPU model or stated compiler, so tier C. Average times are integer nanoseconds (the harness stores uint64 averages), so 6 versus 7 ns is a one-count difference. The baseline is native compiled code of the same expression, not any other expression JIT or interpreter; there is no comparison with exprtk, muparser, tinyexpr or similar, so it shows parity with native code rather than a win over a competitor. An older benchmark summary in analysis/asmd_optimizer_benchmark_summary.csv lists avg_runtime_ns 11 to 12 against compiler_runtime_ns 10 to 11 (column meaning inferred from the names), i.e. mexce slower than native at that earlier stage. The repository's own improvement report (analysis/improvement_report.md, a 35-agent analysis run) lists miscompilation and correctness bugs found on master as of 2026-06-10 (for example B1, a clobbered argument in the SSE2 binary libm call path); whether the README table was measured before or after those fixes is not stated. In the analysis/performance_acceptance.md run the GCC 13.3.0 evaluate medians are 6.9 and 6.5 ns, compared only between mexce commits.

name: Vc (SIMD Vector Classes)
baseline: plain sequential scalar loop built by GCC 5.3.0 with -O3 -ftree-vectorize -ffast-math (compiler auto-vectorization; exp/log/sqrt go through libm)
workload: Euro-Par 2016 SIMD kernels run on one thread over 8192 doubles with AVX2 (SIMD width 4): simple (sqrt/log/exp wrapper), conditional math call, early return, nested branching, and while loop with varying trip count; the Vc 1.2.0 version (simd_class_vectorization) is compared with the sequential reference.
claimed_speedup: Third-party data (mean time per loop iteration, GCC 5.3.0, Haswell, 1 thread, SIMD width 4), Vc vs sequential reference, ratios derived from page data: simple EXP 7.8586e-09 s vs 2.477e-08 s (3.15x), simple LOG 8.14221e-09 vs 3.58324e-08 (4.40x), simple SQRT 6.41381e-09 vs 1.14677e-08 (1.79x); conditional_math_call EXP 2.27x, LOG 2.39x, SQRT 5.07x (3.3077e-09 vs 1.67538e-08); early_return EXP 2.87x, LOG 3.16x, SQRT 4.30x; nested_branching EXP 1.56x, LOG 1.64x, SQRT 2.19x; while_loop EXP 1.34x, LOG 1.62x, SQRT 0.78x (Vc slower: 5.97054e-08 vs 4.6563e-08). Hand-written AVX2 intrinsics and OpenMP 4.x 'omp simd' versions are often equal or faster than Vc in the same logs.
compiler_and_flags: GNU 5.3.0 (glibc 2.22 era), Vc 1.2.0; makefile.gnu in flwende/simd_benchmarks: g++ -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++11 -ftree-vectorize -ffast-math -mavx2 -mfma -D__AVX2__ -DSIMD_WIDTH_LOGICAL_REAL64=4 -DDEBUG, built with -DCONDITIONAL_CALL (notes.txt). The makefile is the master-branch copy and may differ slightly from the August 2016 build.
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2680v3 (Haswell) at 1.9 GHz, Cray aprun with --p-state=1900000
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; packaged in Debian and Arch Linux and listed in CERN LCG
tradeoffs: Explicit SIMD value types (float_v, double_v) written into the code, so algorithms must be restructured for data parallelism; supports x86 SSE2 to AVX2 only (AVX-512, NEON and MIC support removed or never finished); the project is in maintenance mode and points users to std-simd (std::experimental::simd in GCC 11+ libstdc++).
caveats: Vc's own README and docs carry no benchmark numbers; the evidence is third-party data from the Euro-Par 2016 paper 'Portable SIMD Performance with OpenMP 4.x Compiler Directives' (Wende et al.), whose subject is OpenMP, not Vc. The baseline is compiler-generated scalar code with libm calls, not a library facility: the reference loop's exp/log calls may not auto-vectorize on GCC 5.3.0 unless glibc libmvec is used (GLIBC_ROOT is optional in the makefile and notes.txt does not say whether it was set for the hsw runs), so the larger gains may partly measure Vc's vector math against scalar libm. Vc is slower than the reference on while_loop SQRT (0.78x), and only single-thread width-4 AVX2 logs were read here (threads12 and SIMD width 8 logs, Intel and Clang runs not read). The Vc authors' own paper (Kretz and Lindenstruth, Software: Practice and Experience) and Kretz's dissertation were unreachable (host blocked), so no first-party numbers were checked. The data repo has only 9 commits and 6 stars.

name: SLEEF (SIMD Library for Evaluating Elementary Functions)

claimed_speedup: From Table 2 (reciprocal throughput, ns): sin 1-ulp domain [0,1e+100]: FDLIBM 162.3 vs SLEEF 48.79 (~3.3x); cos same domain: 162.1 vs 50.38 (~3.2x); tan same domain: 177.0 vs 48.82 (~3.6x); log domain [0,1e+300]: 31.66 vs 15.46 (~2.0x); exp domain [-700,700]: 12.19 vs 7.663 (~1.6x); on the narrow domain [0.4,0.5] SLEEF is roughly at parity with FDLIBM (e.g. sin: 11.43 vs 11.41). (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: SLEEF and FDLIBM compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -mavx2 -mfma; Vector-libm compiled with gcc-7.3.0 -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize -ftree-vectorizer-verbose=1 -fno-math-errno; SVML via Intel C Compiler 19 with -fimf-max-error=1.0/4.0
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 CPU @ 3.40GHz, Turbo Boost disabled (physical PC, no VM)
tradeoffs: Vectorized code takes the slow path for a whole SIMD register if any lane needs it; library offers a 1-ULP and a faster 3.5-ULP accuracy tier as a speed/accuracy tradeoff; on narrow argument domains the scalar-equivalent speed roughly ties FDLIBM rather than beating it, the win is concentrated in wide-domain/branchy cases and true vector (multi-lane) throughput.
caveats: The paper (IEEE TPDS, peer-reviewed, arXiv preprint used here) compares against FDLIBM, a specific reference libm implementation, not directly against libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::sin/std::exp as shipped, though many system libms derive from similar algorithms; the sleef.org benchmark page itself (https://sleef.org/benchmark.xhtml) only compares against Intel SVML, not libm, so that page was not used as the evidence source. Public availability of the exact benchmark harness used for Table 2 was not independently confirmed in this session, so tier is capped at B rather than A.

Author: 'GLM is the fastest on the HTC Desire with both ABIs' (plain armeabi is a tie: additions 10256 vs 9944, multiplications 59008 vs 59460). Opposite result on the SSE x86 build: Eigen additions 30 vs GLM 76, multiplications 86 vs 400.

tradeoffs: Header-only, GLSL-style API; SIMD paths are opt-in through GLM_FORCE_* configuration and aligned types; no expression templates or lazy evaluation, so chained operations create temporaries. GLM is a graphics-oriented library and not a general linear-algebra package.

Only 4x4 float add and multiply were measured. On the tested Intel CPU with SSE, Eigen is 2.5x (additions) and 4.7x (multiplications) faster than GLM, and the author chose Eigen for that reason. The GLM win is on 2010 phone ARM cores (armeabi-v7a) and the plain armeabi column is a tie. The README's non-SSE laptop column is an -O0 build (GLM 2375/7337 vs Eigen 8065/22404) and is not a meaningful comparison. The README says 1 million matrices times 10 repeats but src/Driver.cpp runs 10 matrices times 1,000,000 repeats. The Eigen test matrices set only the diagonal (off-diagonals not initialised in the generator). Compiler and NDK versions not stated, no repeats or variance. GLM's own test/perf programs only compare its scalar and SIMD paths and publish no numbers; the GLM README has no benchmark section.

name: Klein
baseline: GLM (glm::quat multiplication; glm::dualquat converted with mat3x4_cast and applied to a glm::vec4), with RTM (Realtime Math) as a second reference
workload: Static llvm-mca analysis (100 iterations, dispatch width 6) of the generated SSE assembly for two routines: rotor (quaternion) composition and motor (dual-quaternion) application to a point; not measured run time.
claimed_speedup: docs/perf.md llvm-mca totals per 100 iterations: rotor composition Klein 821 cycles / 2400 instructions vs GLM 1522 cycles / 5700 instructions (1.85x fewer cycles, derived from page data) vs RTM 824 cycles / 2300 instructions (parity); block reciprocal throughput 8.0 vs GLM 14.0 vs RTM 7.0. Motor application to a point: Klein 1831 cycles / 5900 instructions vs GLM dual-quat 5435 cycles / 14100 instructions (2.97x fewer cycles, derived from page data); block reciprocal throughput 13.5 vs 38.5. docs/index.md: 'Klein's performance is fully competitive with state of the art kinematic and math libraries built with traditional vector and quaternion formulations.'
tradeoffs: Specialised to 3D projective geometric algebra P(R*_{3,0,1}) with SSE (SSE3 required, SSE4.1 optional) rather than a general vector library; SSE intrinsics only in this version (README requires an SSE3 processor). Points, lines, planes, rotors and motors share one algebra, so motors replace separate quaternion and dual-quaternion code.
caveats: The only numbers are first-party llvm-mca cycle estimates (the page itself warns they cannot predict real performance); no runtime measurements, compiler version, flags or target CPU are stated, and Klein's source supports mc_ruler microbenchmark builds against GLM and RTM in perf/ but no timing results are published. GLM's assembly is largely scalar with stack spills, so GLM was probably built without its SIMD options (not stated); the GLM motor-application routine includes converting a dual quaternion to a 3x4 matrix on each call, which inflates its count against Klein's direct motor-point application. Against RTM, the best-optimised SIMD baseline, the result is a tie. The project site jeremyong.com/klein, which the README points to for documentation, is blocked here; the docs were read from the repo's docs/ folder. Repo is archived, with the README saying it was paused for lack of time.

name: libdivide
baseline: hardware integer division (compiler-emitted DIV/IDIV with a runtime divisor)
workload: Sum of quotients of an array of random numerators divided by one runtime divisor, scalar, branchfree and SIMD vector variants, from the bundled benchmark program.
claimed_speedup: README: 'a speedup of up to 10x for 64-bit integer division and a speedup of up to 5x for 32-bit integer division', more with SSE2/AVX2/AVX512/NEON/SVE vectors. Sample output in the README (type not stated): hardware divide 9.684 ns versus libdivide scalar 0.792 ns (12.2x derived from page data), branchfree 0.783 ns, vector 0.426 ns (22.7x derived); in rows using the generic algorithm libdivide scalar is 1.355 ns versus 9.078 ns (6.7x derived).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (default for the bundled benchmark) with -march=native when supported and -fno-lax-vector-conversions; compiler not stated for the quoted numbers
tradeoffs: Only pays off when the divisor is a runtime value reused many times (a hot loop); compilers already turn compile-time constant divisors into multiply and shift. Building a divider costs a few to a few tens of nanoseconds (the 'gener' column, 1.3 to 29 ns in the sample). Branchfree divider cannot take unsigned divisor 1 and uses more instructions; signed types are slower than unsigned; x86 64-bit vector division is much slower than 32-bit for lack of a vector multiply.
caveats: First-party claim. The benchmark program is public (test/benchmark.cpp, default type u64) but the README's sample output names no CPU, compiler or integer width, so it is tier C. The README's 90-cycle 64-bit divide latency describes older x86 parts; recent cores have much faster dividers, so the 10x figure is likely smaller on current hardware (not measured here). The baseline is the hardware divide instruction rather than a C++ library facility.

The float sqrtf and expf rows (8 cycles) are artifacts, so no sqrt or exp comparison is valid. The spreadsheet has no column headers (min/avg/max inferred from benchmark.c and interface.c), carries no toolchain versions, and was last edited 2021-05-01 per its metadata, so numbers may predate later code changes. Fixed point is compared with float only, not with another fixed-point library. name: NumKong
baseline: GCC 12 auto-vectorized loops (f32 and _Float16); also NumPy 2.4 + OpenBLAS, PyTorch 2.10 + MKL and JAX 0.9
workload: Single-threaded 2048-d dot products and 2048x2048 matrix multiplication across f64, f32, bf16, f16, e5m2 and i8 on Intel Sapphire Rapids, plus inner product, cosine, Euclidean and Jensen-Shannon kernels on f16 versus GCC 12 auto-vectorized code.
claimed_speedup: Dot product (2048-d): f32 7.1 gso/s versus NumPy+OpenBLAS 1.5 (about 4.7x, derived from page data), PyTorch+MKL 0.6, JAX 0.4; f64 5.8 versus 2.0; f16 11.5 versus 0.2 (NumPy), 0.5 (PyTorch); i8 14.8 versus 1.1 (NumPy, overflowing). Matmul 2048x2048: i8 1279 gso/s versus PyTorch+MKL 50.0; e5m2 398 versus 0.4; but f64 8.6 versus 65.5 (NumPy+OpenBLAS) and 68.2 (PyTorch+MKL), f32 37.7 versus 140 and 145, bf16 458 versus 851 (PyTorch). GCC 12 table: f16 inner product 5,990 K/s versus GCC f16 192 K/s (31x) and GCC f32 3,810 K/s (about 1.6x, derived); Jensen-Shannon f16 2,140 K/s versus GCC f16 18 K/s (118x). Binary size: 5 MB versus NumPy+OpenBLAS 30 MB, JAX 357 MB, PyTorch+MKL 705 MB.
compiler_and_flags: Only 'GCC 12' stated for the auto-vectorization table, no flags; NumPy 2.4, PyTorch 2.10, JAX 0.9 for the library table. The repo builds with -march=x86-64 plus per-function target pragmas and -fno-tree-vectorize for its own serial fallbacks (CONTRIBUTING.md); bench/README.md gives the cmake commands for nk_bench.
hardware: Intel Sapphire Rapids (microarchitecture only, no exact CPU model), single-threaded
tradeoffs: 2,000+ hand-written SIMD kernels across x86, Arm, RISC-V, LoongArch, Power and WebAssembly with runtime dispatch; mixed-precision widening accumulators (f16 to f32, f32 to f64, i8 to i32) and compensated f64 Dot2 summation change numerical results versus plain same-type accumulation; caller-owned threads and buffers; no general BLAS API.
caveats: First-party README tables with partial methodology, so tier C: the CPU is named by microarchitecture only, no flags or run counts for the library tables, and the 'gso/s' unit counts integer and float work together. Baselines are Python frameworks (NumPy, PyTorch, JAX) for the headline tables, not C++ std::vector loops; Python call overhead is part of the single 2048-d dot product row. The matrix multiplication table is mixed: NumKong is slower than OpenBLAS and MKL for f64 (8.6 versus 65.5 and 68.2 gso/s), f32 (37.7 versus 140 and 145) and bf16 (458 versus 851). The GCC 12 comparison uses plain auto-vectorized loops on _Float16, which is a weak baseline; against GCC f32 the f16 kernels win by only about 1.6x on inner product. NumKong's repo-level benchmark (bench/README.md) mostly compares its own SIMD backends against serial code, not other libraries. The sibling NumWars repo (broader cross-library comparisons by the same author) was not opened.

name: SIMD Everywhere
baseline: unvectorized (scalar) implementation of the same program (VVenC/VVdeC ported from x86 SSE/AVX to Arm)
workload: Fraunhofer HHI VVenC encoder and VVdeC decoder (H.266/VVC) whose x86 SSE/AVX intrinsics were translated to Arm Neon automatically through SIMDe, compared with the unvectorized build.
claimed_speedup: More than 200% performance gain over unvectorized code on Arm (search-result text of the Arm Community blog post 'Part 1: Porting to Arm Intrinsics with SIMDe'; snippet only). A separate arXiv paper (2309.16509, 'SIMD Everywhere Optimization from ARM NEON to RISC-V Vector Extensions', snippet only) reports 1.51x to 5.13x over the original SIMDe on XNNPACK for an RVV-enhanced SIMDe, which is a different baseline.
stars_or_usage: 3.1k stars; used by Bowtie 2, MMseqs2, OBS Studio, wabt, vvenc/vvdec, vectorscan, Firefox (WASM SIMD128 builds), plink2 and over 30 other projects listed on its wiki
tradeoffs: Header-only portable implementations of x86 (MMX to AVX-512), NEON, WASM SIMD128 and other intrinsic sets; use the native instruction when available, otherwise a fallback that depends on compiler auto-vectorization (README strongly recommends -O3 and OpenMP SIMD pragmas via -fopenmp-simd or SIMDE_ENABLE_OPENMP). Some fallbacks are slow on a given target and which of two code paths is faster varies by target (wiki FAQ), so porting needs per-target benchmarking. Intel's char-based signatures become int8_t, which can need minor source changes.
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the Arm blog page and arXiv are blocked in this environment, so I could not open them, read the hardware, compiler flags or per-workload breakdown, or confirm that the baseline is a scalar build of the same code; the SIMDe README, wiki (Performance-Tuning, FAQ, Alternatives, Projects-Using-SIMDe) and repo have no benchmark numbers and the repo has no benchmark directory. The Arm blog is a vendor-ecosystem write-up of a Fraunhofer HHI port, not an independent test, and the paper's baseline is SIMDe itself. SIMDe's purpose is portability, so a speedup over scalar code on a non-x86 target is the relevant claim; on x86 with native intrinsics it should simply match them. Needs a second pass from a thread that can open arxiv.org and developer.arm.com.

name: GNU gperf
baseline: std::unordered_map (string-keyed lookup in a fixed keyword set)
workload: qlibs/mph benchmark: ns per lookup of random strings from a fixed key set (5, 6 or 100 keys; lengths 4, 8, 2-5 and 1-8) through a gperf-generated function versus std::unordered_map; separately, constexpr-phf's benchmark on Xapiand's 192 field-type names (mixed length).
claimed_speedup: GNU gperf's own manual and README give no numbers. Third-party numbers (ns/op, gperf vs std::unordered_map), clang++: 5 keys len 8: 7.70 vs 13.45 (1.75x, derived from page data); 6 keys len 2-5: 7.94 vs 15.28 (1.92x, derived); 100 keys len 8: 8.04 vs 15.32 (1.91x, derived); 100 keys len 1-8: 13.06 vs 19.34 (1.48x, derived). g++: 100 keys len 8: 7.75 vs 15.01 (1.94x, derived); 100 keys len 1-8: 11.20 vs 25.35 (2.26x, derived). Counter-example: 5 keys len 4: gperf 7.70 vs unordered_map 5.56 ns/op (clang++) and 7.69 vs 5.29 (g++), i.e. gperf 1.4x slower. Kronuz/constexpr-phf README on 192 field-type names: gperf 14 ns/op vs std::unordered_map 29 ns/op (2.07x, derived from page data) and std::set 82 ns/op.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ and g++ (versions not stated), -std=c++20 -O3 -DNDEBUG -mbmi2 (qlibs/mph benchmark); GCC 11 -O3 on x86_64 (constexpr-phf)
stars_or_usage: GitHub mirror has 0 stars; used by the GNU C, GNU C++, GNU Pascal and GNU Java compilers and GNU indent to recognise reserved words (gperf README and manual)
tradeoffs: Build-time generator that emits C or C++ source (switch or table form) for a fixed keyword set; the generated code is not covered by the GPL (manual, 'The Copyright of the Output'), but the generator is GPL. Works on selected character positions, so it handles small and medium sets well; gsauthof/phashtable's README reports it does not terminate in a reasonable time on 1.4 million ISINs and gave a 10% table fill on smaller sets, and rurban/Perfect-Hash's README says it cannot deal with certain anagrams. Non-minimal tables by default.
caveats: The speedup evidence comes from competing perfect-hash libraries' READMEs (qlibs/mph, Kronuz/constexpr-phf), not from the gperf project, and in both gperf is shown beaten by the authors' own library (mph 1.4-1.6 ns/op on the string rows vs gperf 7.7-13 ns/op). qlibs/mph benchmark code is public (branch 'benchmark') with compiler flags, but the CPU is not stated; constexpr-phf names GCC 11 -O3 but no CPU in the section I read. Random-string key sets only; gperf loses on 5 four-character keys. The original evidence, Schmidt's 1990 USENIX C++ paper 'GPERF: A Perfect Hash Function Generator' (Section 5 benchmarks against other keyword-lookup methods), sits on hosts blocked in this session, so its numbers are not recorded. Home page https://www.gnu.org/software/gperf/ was not reachable; the repo URL is an unofficial GitHub mirror whose latest commit is 2022-02-08 and may lag the GNU Savannah repository.

Derived from page data: 2.3x, 3.0x, 2.7x, 2.3x, 1.5x and 1.2x faster. glibc is faster in 20 of the 32 rows (e.g. qsort_int 2.8x, strtod 4.3x, strstr 2.9x, malloc_free_small 11x, strncmp 37x), 3 rows tie.
compiler_and_flags: zig 0.15.2 (clang 20.1.2) 'zig cc' with -std=c11 -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto=full -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops -DNDEBUG -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math -g0 -s, targets x86_64-linux-gnu and x86_64-linux-musl (run.sh)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Linux 6.8.0-87-generic (Ubuntu 22.04), run dated 2025-11-18
stars_or_usage: 400 stars (kraj/musl, a downstream mirror of the official musl git); benchmark repo 7 stars
tradeoffs: Repo description stresses efficient static and dynamic linking, lightweight code and low runtime overhead rather than peak throughput. In the same table musl's malloc (malloc_free_small 11x, malloc_free_medium 4x slower), qsort (2.8x), strtod (4.3x) and several str* routines (strcpy 5.9x, strncmp 37x slower) lose badly to glibc; musl+jemalloc closes most of the malloc gap. Software relying on glibc-specific behaviour may need porting.
caveats: Weak claim: musl wins only 9 of 32 rows against glibc and loses 20; a faster-than-glibc statement holds only for the rows named. The benchmark is a one-person third-party repo (fereidani/musl-vs-glibc, 7 stars, no licence on the repo page) and is not like for like: the glibc binary comes from zig cc's glibc stubs and the system glibc at run time (dynamic) while musl is linked statically, and -flto=full lets the compiler inline statically linked musl code. The 16 KiB memcpy row (glibc 4043.27 ns vs musl 154.19 ns, 26x) is implausible for a real glibc and should be treated as an artifact. The musl project's own home page, wiki and git host and the etalabs libc comparison were unreachable (egress blocked), so any project-side startup-time or size claims could not be checked. The record is filed under the 'musl' project because the repo itself carries no benchmark.

name: xjb
baseline: Ryu (ulfjack/ryu, the double-to-shortest-string algorithm that std::to_chars uses in libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC STL; std::to_chars itself is not in the benchmark); also benchmarked against Dragonbox, Schubfach and fmt 12.1.0

claimed_speedup: Result file for GCC 13.3.0 on AMD Ryzen 7 7840H, random doubles, cycles per conversion: xjb64 60.5, ryu 142.5, dragonbox_full 105.8, dragonbox_comp 116.2, fmt_full 132.2, schubfach 127.7, zmij 93.9, yy_double 89.9, i.e. about 2.4x faster than Ryu, 1.75x faster than Dragonbox, 2.2x faster than fmt (derived from page data). On Apple M1 with Apple clang 17.0.0 the same chart reads xjb64 31.4, ryu 98.7, fmt_full 98.3, dragonbox_comp 100.4, about 3.1x faster than Ryu (derived from page data). 'random length' dataset, GCC 13.3.0: xjb64 62.9 vs ryu 199.4.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (result file); bench/makefile builds with -O3 -std=c++20 -march=native -DNDEBUG for g++, icpx and clang++
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7840H w/ Radeon 780M Graphics, 5115 MHz reported, Linux x86-64 (also Apple M1, Apple clang 17.0.0)
stars_or_usage: 46 stars; used by ssrJSON and jsoniter-scala per README
tradeoffs: Single-file implementation with lookup tables (full: 15336 bytes double, 1352 bytes float; compressed: 368 and 64 bytes). Derived from Schubfach and produces identical digits to Schubfach (make check in bench). Uses SIMD (NEON, AVX512IFMA paths credited to dougallj and lemire). Output format is its own (for example 1000 prints as '1000.0', 0 as '0.0', NaN as 'nan'), with a separate JSON variant, so it is not a drop-in for std::to_chars. Big-endian is not supported yet; f80, f128 not supported.
caveats: First-party benchmark run by the author; no peer review. The README's license line says MIT but the LICENSE file and the src/ftoa.cpp header are Apache-2.0 (the awesome-cpp list also says Apache-2.0), so the license is recorded as Apache-2.0; the bench/ directory vendors third-party code (schubfach, ryu, dragonbox, fmt, yy, zmij, teju, uscale) under its own licenses, which the library sources do not need. std::to_chars is not benchmarked; Ryu stands in for it, and the Ryu entry prints its own exponent format, so output formats differ across rows. Cycles come from rdtsc, so values are TSC ticks and only ratios are meaningful. In the newer result files (GCC 15.2.0, Clang 21.1.6, Clang 17 on M1) the xjb64_comp, yyjson and jnum rows sit at about 8 cycles in every dataset, barely above the 5-cycle null baseline, which looks like optimized-away work; the GCC 13.3.0 file does not show this and was used for the headline numbers. The xjb64 row is the one cited. Results differ by compiler: with Clang 21.1.6 on the same CPU xjb64 is 71.1 vs ryu 132.5 cycles (about 1.9x), and with GCC 15.2.0 55.7 vs 144.4 (about 2.6x) (derived from page data).

baseline: strtod (C library; the Apple silicon test machine would be using the macOS libc, which the README does not name)
workload: Lemire's simple_fastfloat_benchmark parsing ASCII decimal text into doubles: 100,000 random numbers uniform in [0.0,1.0], the canada.txt dataset (111,126 lines) and the mesh.txt dataset (73,019 lines); one 32-bit run (benchmark32) against strtof.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark output (Apple silicon, 2026-03-03), ffc vs strtod in MB/s: random [0,1] 2149.68 vs 1102.63 (1.95x, derived from page data); canada.txt 1452.90 vs 916.32 (1.59x, derived from page data); mesh.txt 1019.67 vs 605.46 (1.68x, derived from page data). 32-bit run: ffc 2288.40 vs strtof 1160.10 MB/s (1.97x, derived from page data). Versus its own upstream: ffc 2149.68 vs fastfloat 1902.52 MB/s on random numbers (1.13x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: clang for all runs except benchmark32, which the README says ran with gcc; versions and optimisation flags for the benchmark build are not stated (the repo Makefile builds its tests with clang -O3 -std=c99, but that is not the benchmark build)
hardware: Apple silicon; the benchmark prints 'loaded db: as3 (Apple silicon)' and clock readings of about 3.8-4.1 GHz, exact chip model not stated
stars_or_usage: 209 stars; README says valkey (valkey_strtod.h) and a hiredis pull request use it
tradeoffs: Single-header C99 port of fast_float's algorithm (src/ includes a bigint fallback); also parses 32/64-bit integers in bases 2-36 and offers exact fixed-notation double formatting (ffc_format_double_fixed). Needs the length of the input or an end pointer, unlike strtod. Optional macros trade safety for speed: FFC_ROUNDS_TO_NEAREST elides the runtime rounding-mode check (wrong results if code changes the rounding mode), FFC_ENABLE_FLOAT_INLINING speeds up float parsing 7-35% (README) but can slow double parsing by about 2%.
caveats: First-party numbers from one Apple silicon machine; the README shows raw benchmark output only, without compiler versions or flags, and the harness (lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark) is referenced but not opened by me. The baseline is whatever strtod the macOS libc provides, so the roughly 1.6-2x speedup says little about glibc or musl strtod, and no x86 numbers are published (the macro notes mention Linux x86/ARM measurements but give no figures). Most of the win belongs to the fast_float algorithm: ffc is a port and is only 1.06-1.13x faster than C++ fast_float in the same table. The numbers are dated 2026-03-03 while force-inlining and API changes landed later (last commit 2026-10-02), so they may not match the current header. Candidate duplicate or port of fast_float, which is already catalogued.

name: libart (Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: red-black tree (the ART paper's own in-memory red-black-tree implementation, algorithmically what std::map/std::set are built on, but not literally libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::map)
workload: single-threaded lookups of existing random 32-bit-integer keys in an index of 65K, 16M, and 256M keys, both dense and sparse key distributions (also a 12-thread/8-way-software-pipelined variant at 16M keys), from the ART paper's micro-benchmarks
claimed_speedup: ART reaches roughly 7-10x the lookup throughput of the paper's red-black tree across the tested sizes (e.g. ~110M lookups/sec for ART vs roughly 10-15M for RB at 65K dense keys) (derived from page data: read off the Fig. 10 bar chart, values approximate, not exact printed numbers); multi-threaded ART is ~1.2-1.7x faster than a chained hash table depending on key density
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.6 (optimization flags not stated in the text)
hardware: Intel Core i7 3930K, 6 cores/12 threads, 3.2GHz (3.8GHz turbo), 12MB shared L3 cache, 32GB quad-channel DDR3-1600 RAM, Linux 3.2 x86-64
stars_or_usage: 836 stars; ART is used in the HyPer main-memory database and has influenced indexing in several modern OLTP/OLAP engines
tradeoffs: keys are limited to fixed-width binary-comparable encodings (signed integers, floats, and strings all need a transform to sort correctly bitwise); path compression and lazy expansion are required to bound worst-case space to ~52 bytes/key; libart (this repo) is an independent open-source C99 implementation of the paper's algorithm, not the authors' original benchmark artifact
caveats: the paper benchmarks ART against ITS OWN red-black-tree implementation (one of "two textbook data structures"), not against libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::map, so treat this as evidence for the ART algorithm versus red-black trees generally rather than a direct std::map micro-benchmark; numbers were read off a bar chart rather than a printed table, so are approximate; this GitHub repo (libart) is a separate, unaffiliated C implementation of the published algorithm and was not itself benchmarked in the paper

workload: Google's original 2010 btree_bench: random insert/lookup/fulllookup/delete/queueaddrem/mixedaddrem/fifo/forward-iteration of int32, int64, and string keys/values into btree::set/map (node size 256) vs the STL red-black-tree set/map

name: Yomm2
baseline: C++ virtual member function call (closed dispatch via vtable)
metric: latency (average time per dispatched call, unit not stated on the page)
workload: Google Benchmark loop picking a random hierarchy out of 100, then a random object (or two for arity 2) out of 1000 per hierarchy with randomized allocation sizes, and calling one virtual function or the equivalent open method; ordinary-inheritance and virtual-inheritance variants.
claimed_speedup: Only the virtual_ptr rows beat the baseline. docs/benchmarks/v010500.euclid.clang.md (clang 16.0.6, 100 hierarchies of 1000 objects), arity 1 ordinary base: virtual function 60.1, direct virtual ptr 10.5 (ratio 0.18), indirect virtual ptr 12.2 (0.20); arity 2: virtual function 93.2, direct virtual ptr 19.4 (0.21), indirect 20.5 (0.22), i.e. about 5x lower time per call (derived from page data). With virtual inheritance the same rows are 2.1x slower than the virtual function (arity 1: 74.3 vs 156.9). The README states the headline opposite: dispatch with one virtual argument takes 15-30% more time than the equivalent virtual member function.
compiler_and_flags: clang 16.0.6, build type release (CMake Release; exact flags not stated in the result file)
hardware: host 'euclid', '16 X 3300 MHZ CPUs' (CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 382 stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Open (non-intrusive) multi-methods for C++17 with multiple dispatch on several arguments, which virtual functions cannot do; needs class registration and a runtime update() call that builds dispatch tables (about 75K runtime). Plain-reference dispatch costs 9 instructions and 7 memory reads vs 2 and 2 for a virtual call; virtual_ptr is a fat pointer (extra pointer size) that carries the vptr. Dispatch through virtual bases needs a dynamic cast and is 2-5x slower than virtual functions.
caveats: Weak evidence of 'faster'. The repo is archived (2026-03-04) and superseded by Boost.OpenMethod (Boost 1.90); the README now says YOMM2 'was' a library. The author's own text says open methods are almost as fast as virtual functions and 15-30% slower with plain references, and docs/benchmarks show ratios of 1.06-1.62 for the non-virtual_ptr rows (for example arity 1 ordinary base: basic policy 80.4 vs virtual function 60.1). The 0.18-0.22 ratios for virtual_ptr come from a layout effect in the benchmark: the virtual_ptr rows read the vptr from a contiguous vector of fat pointers, while the virtual function row dereferences each randomly chosen heap object, so object cache misses dominate the baseline (tests/benchmarks.cpp, population::draw vs vptr_draw). The result file gives no time unit and no CPU model, and the benchmark source disables g++ ('Don't benchmark g++ until this is fixed'). The 'much faster than other implementations' claim in docs/articles/performance.md has no numbers. First-party measurement, so tier C.
found_via: seed-list mining backfill: awesome-cpp list entry Yomm2 (https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Frameworks), repo README, ORIGINAL-README.md, docs/articles/performance.md and docs/benchmarks

name: Pairing Heap (priority-queue-testing benchmark suite)
workload: Randomized insert-delete (heap capacity c=1024) and Dijkstra's algorithm on the USA road network, from Larkin/Sen/Tarjan, 'A Back-to-Basics Empirical Study of Priority Queues' (ALENEX 2014).
claimed_speedup: Randomized insert-delete, c=1024: pairing heap 1.00x (fastest) vs implicit-2 (plain binary heap) at 11.87x (i.e. binary heap took 11.87x longer). Dijkstra on USA road map: pairing 1.68x vs implicit-2 3.84x baseline time (~2.3x faster). Sorting: pairing 4.29x vs implicit-2 4.75x (modest win only).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O4
hardware: Dell PowerEdge SC1435, dual AMD Opteron 2212 (dual-core, 2.0GHz, 64KB L1 / 1MB L2 per core), 8GB DDR2-667, Springdale/PUIAS Linux, kernel 2.6.32
stars_or_usage: 2 stars (GitHub mirror of the defunct code.google.com/p/priority-queue-testing, the benchmark suite behind the ALENEX 2014 paper)
tradeoffs: Pairing heap's edge is workload-specific: it dominates on randomized insert-delete and Dijkstra but only modestly beats binary heap on plain sorting, and loses ground on some decrease-key-heavy patterns to other specialized heaps. Comparison is against the paper's own C99 'implicit-2' binary heap (algorithmically identical to std::priority_queue's array-based heap), not literally against libstdc++/libc++'s container.
caveats: 2014-era hardware (AMD Opteron 2212), gcc -O4 with no stated vectorization flags. Repo is an unmaintained auto-export of a shut-down Google Code project, no license file. Paper's headline finding is nuanced -- simple binary heaps remain competitive overall; pairing heap's big wins are specific to certain workloads.

name: prio_queue (rollbear)

name: radix-heap (pair_radix_heap)
workload: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm on real USA road networks (264K to 24M vertices, DIMACS challenge-9 datasets), averaged over 100 random sources; measures both pure priority-queue time and overall algorithm time
claimed_speedup: up to ~1.7x faster on the pure priority-queue workload (e.g. USA.gr: rheap 1.222667s vs stl 2.119727s) and ~1.25-1.29x faster on overall Dijkstra time including edge traversal (derived from page data)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2690 0 @ 2.90GHz, 256GB RAM, Linux 3.2.0
tradeoffs: radix heap is a monotone priority queue: popped keys must be non-decreasing, so it only supports algorithms like Dijkstra with non-negative edge weights, not general priority-queue use; not a drop-in std::priority_queue replacement
caveats: Benchmark dates to 2015 on hardware/compiler of that era; no LICENSE file in repo so code is reference-only, not confirmed redistributable; repo has had no commits since 2015
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "radix heap" (variation on seed query "heap faster than std::priority_queue benchmark")

name: SimdQuickHeap
workload: MonotoneConstantSize workload, i64 keys, n=2^25: build heap via (push∘pop∘push)^n, then 10n interleaved pop/push operations with monotone-increasing keys, timed per element.
claimed_speedup: SimdQuickHeapAvx2: 35.6 ns/elem vs BinaryHeap (Rust std) 439.6 ns/elem = 12.3x faster; SimdQuickHeapAvx512: 32.2 ns/elem = 13.6x faster (both on the monotone-workload sweet spot). More generally: 1.2-1.7x faster than the monotone radix heap and 1.4-2.8x faster than S3Q (superscalar sample queue), the fastest general comparison-based competitor tested.
compiler_and_flags: C++ competitors: Clang, -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native -flto. Rust: release mode, target-cpu=native, full LTO, single codegen unit.
hardware: AMD Zen 4 EPYC 9684X (92 cores, 32 KiB L1d, 1 MiB L2, 32+64 MiB L3 per 8-core package), 12-channel DDR5, Rocky Linux 9.4
tradeoffs: The 12-13x figure is on a monotone-key workload engineered to be near-degenerate for comparison-based heaps; the general win over the next-best rival (S3Q) is a more modest 1.4-2.8x. Needs AVX2/AVX512 for full speed. No run against an actual GCC/Clang/MSVC std::priority_queue was performed -- only against Rust's std::collections::BinaryHeap and several boost::heap variants.
caveats: Published at ESA 2026 (DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2026.16); very recent, no independent replication yet. Largest multiplier is against Rust's own BinaryHeap, not against libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::priority_queue.

name: Superscalar Sample Queue (S3Q)
workload: Random Sort / Random Wiggle push+pop microbenchmark, N from 2^13 to 2^27 elements, measuring (T_insert + T_deleteMin) / (2 log N) in nanoseconds.
claimed_speedup: S3Q obtains speedups over min(S3QBH tuned binary heap, StdQueue = GCC's std::priority_queue) that grow roughly logarithmically with N, reaching 4.6x-7x for the largest instances (2^13-2^27 elements).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.3.0-17ubuntu1~20.04, -O3 (deliberately no -march=native), Ubuntu 20.04.2 LTS, Linux 5.4.0-72-generic
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2650 v2 (Ivy Bridge EP) and AMD Athlon II X4 635 (K10), both x86-64
tradeoffs: Comparison-based, no monotonicity requirement (unlike radix heaps). Loses to Sequence Heap on measured cache-miss counts even though it wins on wall-clock time in this thesis. Later beaten itself by SimdQuickHeap (1.4-2.8x). Header-only C++17, depends on ips4o/range-v3/xoshiro.
caveats: Numbers come from a 2021 KIT master's thesis (not a peer-reviewed venue), though methodology -- code, compiler, exact hardware -- is fully specified, satisfying tier A. 'StdQueue' in the thesis is literally the std::priority_queue shipped with the author's GCC build, the most direct C++-stdlib comparison in this set.

name: RadixHeap (radix_heap_rust)
workload: Criterion benchmark pushing/popping random u32 keys in a monotone extraction pattern, input sizes 125K-64M elements, vs Rust's std::collections::BinaryHeap (with Reverse).
claimed_speedup: ~1.7-2x faster than BinaryHeap across sizes: 1M elems ~180ms vs ~320ms; 8M ~1.6s vs ~3.0s; 64M ~15s vs ~28s.

name: cpp_batched_random
workload: Fisher-Yates array shuffle across a range of array lengths (64-bit elements), using batched multiplication-based random-index generation instead of one RNG call + division per swap; tested with Lehmer, PCG64 and ChaCha generators feeding the shuffle.
claimed_speedup: On Intel Xeon Gold 6338: 1.4-1.8x (Lehmer generator), 1.8-2.5x (PCG64), 2.9-4.7x (ChaCha). On Apple M2: 1.5-2.3x (Lehmer), 1.9-2.6x (PCG64), 2.6-3.9x (ChaCha), all vs an unbatched std::shuffle-equivalent Fisher-Yates baseline
compiler_and_flags: LLVM 16 (Intel Xeon Gold 6338 system); Apple/LLVM 14 (Apple M2 system)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6338 @ 3.2GHz (Ice Lake, DDR4-3200, 48MiB LLC); Apple M2 @ 3.49GHz (Avalanche, LPDDR5-6400, 16MiB LLC)
tradeoffs: Only benefits shuffles driven by a 64-bit-output RNG (e.g. std::mt19937_64); speed advantage shrinks for very large arrays and grows for small/medium ones; adds an extra header dependency vs calling std::shuffle directly.
caveats: Peer-reviewed numbers (Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 2024, arXiv:2408.06213) were measured for the paper's C reference implementation (github.com/lemire/batched_random), not literally this C++ header repo; however this repo (cpp_batched_random) is explicitly the C++ port whose own README states it is 'a drop-in replacement for std::shuffle when the random number generator produces 64-bit integers (e.g. std::mt19937_64)', and its own benchmarks/benchmark.cpp directly compares std::shuffle+std::mt19937_64 against batched_random::shuffle using the same algorithm.

name: PCG (pcg-cpp)
workload: Raw 32-bit/64-bit integer generation, mean time per generation over 100 repetitions, no downstream distribution.
claimed_speedup: pcg_cpp::pcg32_fast: 1071.97M gen/s vs std::mt19937: 270.65M gen/s (~3.96x, derived from page data); pcg_cpp::pcg64_fast: 763.50M gen/s vs std::mt19937_64: 294.26M gen/s (~2.59x, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang, -O3 -DNDEBUG, no architecture-specific optimization flags
hardware: Intel Core i5-3570 @ 3.40GHz
tradeoffs: 128-bit internal state (vs MT19937's ~20,000-bit state) gives far fewer theoretically independent streams; fast variants (pcg32_fast/pcg64_fast) drop the increment-based stream selection used by the 'oneseq'/default variants for extra speed, trading some statistical/stream-separation guarantees; not cryptographically secure; API differs from a drop-in std::mt19937 substitute (template-heavy, many variant typedefs).
caveats: Numbers come from a third-party shootout run on a 2012-era CPU (i5-3570, no AVX2); the README does not state whether libstdc++ or libc++ was linked for the std::mt19937 baseline. pcg-cpp's own site (pcg-random.org, docs pages) makes only statistical-quality benchmarking claims, not speed claims, on the pages checked this session.

name: Random123
workload: Single-chip raw random byte-stream generation throughput (GB/s) and cycles-per-byte, counter-based generators (Philox, Threefry, ARS) vs conventional PRNGs including the C++0x std::mt19937_64.
claimed_speedup: ARS-7 (AES-NI hardware-accelerated): 11.1 GB/s vs std::mt19937_64: 6.1 GB/s (~1.8x, derived from page data) on the Intel CPU tested; Threefry-4x64-20 (no special hardware needed): 6.4 GB/s vs 6.1 GB/s (~1.05x, derived from page data, i.e. only marginally faster without AES-NI)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.5.3 (Intel CPU build)
hardware: 3.07GHz quad-core Intel Xeon X5667 (Westmere)
tradeoffs: Counter-based API (application manages key + counter explicitly) is a different programming model than a stateful std::mt19937 engine, so it is not a drop-in engine substitute without an adapter; the standout CPU speedup (ARS-7) needs AES-NI hardware support -- without it, gains over std::mt19937_64 on CPU are small; largest wins shown in the paper are on GPU, not directly relevant to a CPU std::mt19937 comparison.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (Salmon, Moraes, Dror & Shaw, 'Parallel Random Numbers: As Easy as 1,2,3', SC11, Best Paper Award) with public code and a benchmark table (Table 2) stating CPU model and compiler; however the benchmark hardware is from 2011 (Westmere-era Xeon) and results for most counter-based generators vs std::mt19937_64 on CPU (without AES-NI) are close to a tie, not a large win. GitHub's license detector reports 'Other/NOASSERTION' for this repo even though the LICENSE file text is a standard BSD-3-Clause license.

name: xoshiro_cpp (david-cortes)
workload: Raw 64-bit integer generation (xoshiro256++ variant), mean time per generation over 100 repetitions.
claimed_speedup: xoshiro256++: 946.70M gen/s vs std::mt19937_64: 294.26M gen/s (~3.22x, derived from page data)

Cairo is slower on most other rows, for example Source In 1,069,900 vs 290,673 (Skia AVX2), Screen 3,814,683 vs 311,738, bilinear pattern 17,396,620 vs 2,979,746 and AA hairline 13,508,248 vs 1,855,764. The tiny-skia README itself says only that tiny-skia is faster than cairo and raqote 'in many cases'.
compiler_and_flags: cairo v1.16.0 built with gcc -march=native (the Gentoo system build; gcc version and -O level not stated); Skia m90 built with clang 13, -march=haswell for the AVX2 numbers and -march=x86-64 for the SSE2 numbers, with -DSK_FORCE_RASTER_PIPELINE_BLITTER; benchmarks are Rust 1.62 nightly cargo bench using cairo-rs 0.8 bindings (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/linebender/tiny-skia/HEAD/benches/README.md)
hardware: AMD 3700X on Gentoo Linux (x86-64 results page); an Apple M1 ARM page also exists but was not used here
tradeoffs: Dual-licensed LGPL-2.1 or MPL-1.1 C library with a full vector API and PDF, PS, SVG and X11 backends, so it carries more machinery than a pure rasterizer. Its image backend gets its speed from pixman's hand-tuned SIMD fast paths for simple Porter-Duff operators (Over, Add, Over-reverse) and rectangles; the non-separable and separable blend modes, bilinear and high-quality filters, and anti-aliased hairlines go through slow generic paths.
caveats: This is a mixed result in a competitor's suite (the tiny-skia author runs it to show tiny-skia, not Cairo, in the best light). Cairo is slower than Skia AVX2 on most rows, roughly 3.7x on Source In, 12x on Screen, 5x on Hue, 5.8x on bilinear patterns and 7.3x on AA hairlines (derived from page data), and the bicubic row compares cairo's Gaussian 'best' filter with Skia's bicubic. Skia is built with SK_FORCE_RASTER_PIPELINE_BLITTER, which forces its generic raster-pipeline blitter instead of its hand-tuned legacy paths, so the Skia baseline is not Skia at its fastest for simple operators. The Cairo 'Rect' row leaves antialiasing at the cairo default for fractional rectangle coordinates while the tiny-skia row uses anti_alias=false, so it is not like-for-like. Modulate is unsupported in cairo (reported as 0). Cairo 1.16.0 is from 2018 and the run used Rust 1.62 (2022), so the numbers do not reflect Cairo 1.18. The linebender.github.io results page was EGRESS_BLOCKED; the numbers were read from the page's source on the gh-pages branch at the raw.githubusercontent.com URL (same data), and the benchmark code in tiny-skia/benches/src (blend.rs, fill.rs, patterns.rs) was read. The Cairo site and gitlab.freedesktop.org were also EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the repo URL, last commit date and star count could not be opened; the licence comes from a distro package listing in a search result (Cairo 1.18.2). The pixman build used under cairo is not described.

name: PCRE2
workload: Find-and-count non-overlapping matches of email/URI/IPv4 patterns over a ~concatenated text corpus (learnxinyminutes docs), default engine settings, compiled C++ STL std::regex vs C PCRE2 (10.36-2) via -lpcre2-8.
claimed_speedup: Default build: 4.07x faster total (C++ STL 1023.49ms vs C PCRE2 251.37ms: email 433.09->126.10ms, URI 344.74->112.17ms, IP 245.66->13.10ms). Optimized branch: 11.6x faster (C++ STL 1021.10ms vs PCRE2 87.87ms) (derived from page data: ratios computed from the stated ms totals).
compiler_and_flags: std::regex: g++ 7.5.0, `-std=c++11 -O3`. PCRE2: gcc 7.5.0, `-O3 -DNDEBUG`, linked against PCRE2 10.36-2 (-lpcre2-8). Both run inside the project's Docker image.
hardware: MacBook Pro (16-inch, 2019), 2.4 GHz Intel Core i9, 32 GB 2667 MHz DDR4, macOS Big Sur 11.2.3 (host running the Docker container)
stars_or_usage: 1,362 stars; used as the regex engine in PHP, Apache httpd, Nginx (via a bundled copy), Wireshark, and many other projects
tradeoffs: C API (manual pattern/match-data lifetime management, no RAII) vs std::regex's C++ object model; PCRE (Perl-compatible) syntax has some divergences from the ECMAScript grammar std::regex uses; JIT compilation is an optional extra build/runtime step that widens the speed gap further but adds complexity; requires linking an external C library instead of header-only stdlib usage.
caveats: This benchmark only exercises libstdc++'s std::regex (g++ 7.5.0 inside a Linux container); libc++ and MSVC STL are not tested, so the win is not shown against all three stdlib implementations. Patterns are simple (email/URI/IPv4) over one fixed text corpus, not a broad workload. A separate, less-detailed independent shootout (github.com/xis19/regexp_benchmark, opened this session) shows the same qualitative gap for the older PCRE (8.38, pre-PCRE2) vs std::regex on 10 small patterns, but without stated compiler/hardware, so it is not used as primary evidence here.

Also faster than RE2 in every case it supports (2.90x-16.34x on x86-64, 2.41x-11.53x on arm64) and beats PCRE2-JIT on 7 of 12 patterns on both ISAs.

name: TRE
workload: Find all matches of 15 regex patterns over a ~20 MB English e-book (mtent12.txt), best of 5 runs per engine, wall time in ms, compiled with default engine options.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, not a project claim: on x86-64 Intel Xeon 2.67GHz TRE 0.8.0 beats PCRE2 10.10 on [a-zA-Z]+ing (954 ms vs 1373 ms, 1.44x, derived from page data) and .{0,2}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) (3425 ms vs 5164 ms, 1.51x, derived from page data), ties on .{2,4}(Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn) (5248 ms vs 5298 ms). 32-bit Xeon run: 892 ms vs 1740 ms (1.95x derived), 3641 ms vs 6726 ms (1.85x derived), 5700 ms vs 7107 ms (1.25x derived). TRE is slower than PCRE2 on the other 12 of 15 patterns (e.g. Twain 486 ms vs 5 ms).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.8.2 (Linux) / GCC 4.4.7 (Windows run), engines and harness built with -g -O3 -Wall; TRE called via tre_regcomp(REG_EXTENDED|REG_NEWLINE) and tre_regnexec, PCRE2 via pcre2_compile(PCRE2_MULTILINE)/pcre2_match
hardware: Intel Xeon 2.67GHz (Linux, 64-bit and 32-bit runs); Intel Core i5 3.2GHz (Windows); exact CPU SKU not stated
tradeoffs: POSIX leftmost-longest matching with correct submatches, approximate (agrep-style) matching, wide-char and binary-safe APIs, thread safe, regexec does not allocate from the heap (README). No Perl-style backtracking semantics, so results can differ from PCRE2 on alternation; backreferences are exponential.
caveats: The evidence is a third-party comparison page by the author of the PCRE2 sljit JIT (Zoltan Herczeg, page last modified 2015-08-23), not a TRE claim. TRE loses on 12 of 15 patterns against plain PCRE2, and by 10x to 150x against PCRE2-JIT, Oniguruma and RE2 on many patterns; its two wins are on [a-zA-Z]+ing and the .{0,2}(alternation) pattern, and .{2,4}(alternation) is a 1 percent tie (a loss in the Windows run). Versions are TRE 0.8.0 and PCRE2 10.10 from 2015; current TRE and PCRE2 were not measured. Engines were not tuned (default options). PCRE2 uses leftmost-first Perl semantics and TRE leftmost-longest POSIX semantics, so match counts may differ. Benchmark harness is public as regex-test.tgz on the same gh-pages branch (read in this session: main.c, tre.c, pcre2.c, Makefile, MakeGlobals); tier A except the CPU is given only as 'Intel Xeon 2.67GHz'. name: ankerl::svector (martinus/svector)
workload: Small-vector micro-benchmarks with nanobench, one container per process, median of 9 processes: building 7 inline elements, push_back, emplace_back and insert of std::string, random access, swap, shuffle and sort of 1000 std::string; also object size (sizeof 8 bytes holding 7 inline uint8_t).
claimed_speedup: Build 7 inline elements: 1.26 ns per element vs std::vector 3.85 ns (about 3.1x, derived from page data); insert at front of std::string vector 1320.2 ns vs 1415.2 ns (about 7%); shuffle plus sort of 1000 std::string 31305 ns vs 35435 ns (12%, the only gap the README says exceeds run-to-run noise); emplace_back std::string 22.64 ns vs 23.52 ns (within noise). Slower than std::vector at push_back uint8_t (0.66 vs 0.30 ns, 2.2x), random operator[] (0.67 vs 0.57 ns) and swap of 7 inline uint64_t (2.15 vs 1.66 ns). Object size 8 bytes with 7 inline uint8_t vs 24 bytes with none for std::vector.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 16.1.1, -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG, boost 1.90.0, abseil 20260107.1; meson release build
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, pinned to one core with taskset
tradeoffs: Tagged-pointer design: one byte of overhead, 7 inline bytes in an 8-byte object, at most 127 inline elements, little-endian targets only, no fancy-pointer allocators, move is noexcept only when the element move is, insert of several elements gives only the basic guarantee. Every operation branches on direct or indirect mode, which costs instructions on bookkeeping-only operations. Swap is element-wise for inline storage, not three pointer exchanges.
caveats: The win over std::vector is concentrated in workloads that stay inside the inline storage (std::vector must allocate) and in std::string element work; on pure bookkeeping with trivially copyable elements svector loses to std::vector (push_back 2.2x slower, subscript about 18% slower, swap slower) and loses to absl::InlinedVector at filling inline storage (0.48 ns per element). Several differences are inside the stated run-to-run spread (3% to 7%), and the README marks a winner only where the gap exceeds it. The last commit date is a dependabot bump; the last functional commit is 2026-08-05. libstdc++ is implied by gcc, not stated. Young container maintained by one person.

name: plf::colony (plf::hive)
workload: Independent microbenchmark suite (fill/back-insertion, linear search, random insert, randomized iterate-and-erase at 1%/50% erasure probability, sort, destruction) across element sizes from 8B to 4096B on GCC/libstdc++.
claimed_speedup: "three orders of magnitude faster than the vector and deque" at 1% random erasure with 1024B elements; "about 361'143 times faster than the vector" at 50% random erasure with large elements (verbatim from post); colony reported ~3x SLOWER than std::vector-with-reserve for simple 32B fill/back-insertion.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.9.4, -std=c++11 -march=native -O2
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 @ 3.4GHz, Gentoo Linux
tradeoffs: Unordered container: element insertion order is not preserved and elements are not indexable by position like vector's operator[]; higher per-element memory overhead (skip-field metadata) than vector; key advantage is that erase() never invalidates other iterators/pointers/references (unlike vector/deque), which is what makes bulk random erasure O(1) per element instead of O(n).
caveats: Benchmark dated 2017 on GCC 4.9.4 (dated compiler); the headline 361,143x figure is specific to a 50%-random-erasure iterate/erase workload on large (multi-KB) elements at whatever container size the author's graph reached, and reflects colony's O(1) erase vs. vector/deque's O(n) erase-and-shift -- an asymptotic-complexity artifact, not a representative 'typical workload' multiplier; for simple sequential fill of small/medium elements the same post reports colony as slower than std::vector. Only libstdc++ (GCC) was exercised in this post, not libc++ or MSVC STL. The library's own site (plflib.org/colony.htm, colony v6.11, GCC 9.2 x64, Intel Xeon E3-1241 Haswell, -O2 -march=native, benchmark source in the colony downloads section) shows qualitatively consistent rankings (colony/list leading insertion and erasure, vector leading iteration) but presents numbers as graph images rather than machine-readable text, so it was used only as corroboration, not the primary citation. The library has since been forked/renamed to plf::hive (github.com/mattreecebentley/plf_hive, 179 stars, also active) to track the pending std::hive standardization proposal (P0447); both repos are maintained in parallel by the same author and the cited benchmark evidence applies to both implementations.

name: CTL (C Container Template Library)
baseline: libstdc++ containers (std::vector, std::list, std::deque, std::set, std::unordered_set, std::string) from g++ 10.2.1
workload: tests/perf microbenchmarks with int elements, sizes up to about 25,000: push_back, pop_back, push_front, iterate, sort, insert, erase and clear per container, plus a compile-time and memory bar chart of the C11 build against the C++ STL build.
claimed_speedup: The README gives no ratio in text; its log-scale PNG plots show CTL as solid lines and the STL as dotted lines. Read off the plots at 25k elements (approximate, derived from page data): CTL roughly equal to the STL for vector, list, deque, set and unordered_set push, pop, insert, erase and iterate; str push_back about 3x faster than std::string push_back; sorts slower (vector sort about 1.5x, deque sort about 2x, string sort about 30x slower). The compile chart labels CTL 'tests/perf/perf_compile_c11.c' 60.12 KB and 117752k RSS against 'perf_compile_cc.cc' 43.944 KB and 153612k RSS (about 23% less compiler memory, derived from page data), with both bars at about 1.7 s.
compiler_and_flags: g++ (GCC) 10.2.1 20201125 (Red Hat 10.2.1-9), -O3 -march=native (from the plot titles)
tradeoffs: Header-only macro-templated containers for C99/C11 (one include per element type), 24 container types, fat bounds-checked iterators, default max_size of 2^32 bytes and anti-DoS hash policies; the unordered_set uses a security-oriented collision policy that trades speed for safety. Only the lower-than comparator is officially supported with algorithms.
caveats: This is a weak claim: the project's stated goal is fast compiling and STL-compatible behaviour, and the plots show parity rather than wins, with sorts clearly slower. The unordered_set doc says 'Overall the STL unordered_set performance is bad, and our is also not much better.' The compile chart shows equal compile time (about 1.7 s each) and a larger CTL object (60.12 KB vs 43.944 KB), with only compiler memory lower. No ratio appears in text; all figures were read off embedded PNG plots (docs/images/*.log.png), so they are approximate. Hardware is not stated, the compiler is old (GCC 10.2.1, 2020), and results are first-party. Only int (and std::string) elements are measured. As the README notes, the C++ functions are dynamically loaded from libstdc++.so.6 while the C versions are linked into the binary. Continuation of glouw/ctl (1.4k stars, MIT) per the README, which lists a renamed API and 254 methods as improvements over the original; GitHub fork status was not confirmed from the page.

name: mpack
workload: Encode (write), tree-parse and incremental-parse of randomly generated schemaless objects (2367-byte 'small' and 248571-byte 'large' MessagePack documents with mixed maps, arrays, strings, ints, doubles), hash time subtracted.
claimed_speedup: Write, small: MPack 2.13 us vs msgpack C 6.42 us and msgpack C++ 2.77 us. Write, large: 307.27 us vs 544.24 us (C) and 347.14 us (C++). Tree parse, small: MPack 4.99 us vs msgpack C 6.47 us and msgpack C++ 9.40 us. Tree parse, large: 414.16 us vs 750.87 us (C) and 1004.67 us (C++). Derived from page data: encode 3.0x (small) and 1.8x (large) over msgpack C, 1.3x and 1.1x over msgpack C++; tree parse 1.3x and 1.8x over msgpack C, 1.9x and 2.4x over msgpack C++. README: 'MPack outperforms all JSON and MessagePack libraries (except CWPack), and in some tests MPack is several times faster than RapidJSON'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3.0 on Arch Linux; -Wall -O3 -flto -fno-fat-lto-objects -DPIC -fPIC -DNDEBUG (-O3 and -flto always enforced)
hardware: AMD Phenom(tm) II X6 1090T (x86_64, 6402 bogomips) desktop PC; also a first-generation Raspberry Pi table
tradeoffs: C library, amalgamation (mpack.h and mpack.c) embeddable, runs on 8-bit microcontrollers and in the Linux kernel; MessagePack only (not a JSON drop-in); stateful error handling instead of per-call return codes; tree API gives an immutable node tree; README recommends the Expect API (known schema) for maximum performance, which that suite does not cover.
caveats: Benchmark is written and run by the MPack author (the suite's own disclaimer says it may be biased). Benchmarked MPack is 0.8.1 and msgpack-c 1.3.0 (2016-era, GCC 5.3.0, Phenom II) while the README now describes MPack 1.1 and msgpack-c 3.3.0, so current ratios are unknown. Tree-parse and incremental rows are not all wins: libbson's tree row is faster (4.45 us small, 301.90 us large) and libbson is BSON not MessagePack. The README claim 'except CWPack' is not backed by the suite README, which lists CMP, msgpack and MPack as MessagePack implementations but not CWPack. msgpack C encode row (6.42 us) is the weakest baseline; msgpack C++ is only 1.1x to 1.3x behind on writes. Ratios are derived from the page tables.

name: pbtools
baseline: Google Protocol Buffers C++ (libprotobuf 3.6.1) and protobuf-c
workload: Encode and decode of two protobuf messages from Google's benchmark proto ('Message' wrapping Message1 with 566-byte wire size, and Message3 with 106-byte wire size), 2,000,000 iterations each, per library.
claimed_speedup: Encoding: pbtools -O2 1.457 s vs Google protobuf C++ -O3 2.231 s (about 1.53x faster, derived from page data) and vs protobuf-c -O3 1.892 s (about 1.30x, derived from page data). Decoding: pbtools -O2 1.594 s vs Google -O3 1.997 s (about 1.25x, derived from page data) and vs protobuf-c -O3 2.508 s (about 1.57x, derived from page data). With -O2 -flto pbtools encodes in 1.319 s and decodes in 1.239 s. At -Os pbtools is not ahead on encoding (3.398 s vs protobuf-c 1.970 s, Google 3.713 s).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.3.0; per-row flags in the README tables: pbtools -O2 / -O2 -flto / -Os / -Os -flto, protobuf-c and Google -O3 / -Os (protobuf-c also -flto); common CFLAGS -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wl,--gc-sections (benchmark/common.mk)
hardware: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-4510U CPU @ 2.00GHz
tradeoffs: Generates C source from proto3 files with a Python generator; no malloc/free, all allocations come from a caller-supplied workspace (arena) that cannot be freed, so repeated-field lengths cannot change after allocation; generates functions instead of tables, so executable size grows faster than table-driven libraries (README: text 17484 B vs nanopb 21256 B for the benchmark program, but growth is steeper); proto3 only, options, services (gRPC), reserved fields and public imports are not implemented; char must be 8 bits.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party and the toolchain is old (gcc 8.3.0, Google protobuf C++ libprotoc 3.6.1, protobuf-c version not stated), so the Google C++ numbers predate current protobuf releases. The README rows list -O3 for Google and protobuf-c, but the committed benchmark/common.mk sets OPT_SPEED = -O2, so the exact flags per row could not be reproduced from the Makefiles alone. The libraries use different memory models: pbtools builds and decodes into a fixed stack workspace with no malloc, protobuf-c mallocs and frees per iteration, Google C++ reuses one message object on decode and serializes to std::string; the encode loops include building the message, so the comparison favours the arena design. The headline win vanishes at -Os (pbtools encode 3.398 s vs protobuf-c 1.970 s). FlatBuffers decodes in 0.100 s (-O2) but only because it decodes lazily and the benchmark uses fields once. Single machine, single run per row, no variance reported, small messages only. The repo's guessed baseline (msgpack) is wrong: msgpack is not in the benchmark. Project has had no commits since 2023-06-04.
