name: BitSerializer
workload: Fields per millisecond saving a C++ test model (array of objects with 10 fields each: bool, int8, uint64, float, double and five strings including long, Russian Unicode, escaped and multi-line values) to an in-memory std::string and loading it back, MsgPack format; best (minimum) time over a 30 second window per stage, thread pinned to one core.
claimed_speedup: BitSerializer-MsgPack vs NlohmannJson-MsgPack: save to memory 86842 vs 2621 fields/ms (about 33x, derived from page data), load from memory 49254 vs 2206 fields/ms (about 22x, derived from page data). README also says the built-in JSON archive is about 40% faster than BitSerializer's own RapidJSON-based JSON archive, and that wrapped third-party formats (RapidJSON, PugiXml, RapidYAML) cost about 5% against their native APIs.
tradeoffs: Header-style C++17 library; types need a Serialize function or KeyValue mapping per class (non-intrusive). MsgPack, CSV and the new built-in JSON archive have no external dependencies; the RapidJSON, PugiXml and RapidYAML archives pull in those libraries. Streams straight to and from the model with no intermediate DOM, so it cannot do arbitrary DOM manipulation the way nlohmann::json can.
caveats: Benchmark source is public (benchmarks/archives, with a CMake target and competitors/*.h) but no compiler, flags or CPU model are stated anywhere in the repo or README, and the committed report JSON and chart carry no machine information, so it is a first-party result with partial methodology (tier C, not A). The only nlohmann::json row is MsgPack; there is no nlohmann JSON text row in the committed report. The baseline builds a nlohmann::json DOM and converts it, while BitSerializer maps the struct straight to bytes, which the README itself calls not entirely fair ('Serialization' vs 'Parser' classes). Output equivalence is not checked: the committed output-size report does not include the nlohmann MsgPack row. Against RapidJSON, PugiXml and RapidYAML the BitSerializer archives are within about 5% or slightly slower, not faster (RapidJson save 14103 vs 13636, load 11957 vs 11149 fields/ms), so the speedup claim holds only for MsgPack against nlohmann. The 33x and 22x ratios are derived from the report's two numbers.

name: protobuf-c
workload: Encode plus decode round trip of one 494-byte protobuf message (all scalar widths, floats, strings, bytes, eight numeric arrays, a nested struct, an array of structs, Unicode strings); each timed iteration re-encodes the freshly decoded message; best of 5 runs; embedded-category host build.
claimed_speedup: protobuf-c 328.0 MB/s (663,929 msg/s) vs nanopb 61.9 MB/s (125,240 msg/s), about 5.3x faster on both metrics (derived from page data). No msgpack comparison found.
compiler_and_flags: Embedded targets are built for size with -Os -flto (README); C compiler and version not stated
tradeoffs: Wire-compatible with Google protobuf, so it needs protoc plus protoc-gen-c and a C runtime; decoded messages are allocated through a pluggable allocator (malloc by default), unlike nanopb's static allocation; the arena README calls it 'desktop-class' and ranks it for reference against footprint-oriented nanopb, so code size is larger than nanopb's.
caveats: Third-party numbers from a rival codec's benchmark arena (SofaBuffers), where protobuf-c is a reference row and not the subject; the author of that arena has an interest in the result. Host CPU, OS and compiler version are not stated, so the run is not reproducible as published (harness code is public). The rows are -Os size-optimized host builds of the embedded codecs, not speed builds, and the 5.3x ratio is derived by comparing two rows of one table. One message shape only. msgpack was not tested in that arena. The GLD.SerializerBenchmark C suite also lists protobuf-c, but its own docs say the protobuf-c row times a shared in-tree proto3 wire codec rather than protobuf-c itself, so it was not used as evidence. No benchmark or performance numbers exist in the protobuf-c README or repo root; issue #394 (nested-message copies) quotes no timings. Last commit April 2025 (release 1.5.2), and the GLD suite author filed a benchmark-fairness request (#803, July 2026) and a spec-compliance report (#810, September 2026) on its issue tracker.

name: Protocol Puffers (protopuf)
baseline: Google protobuf C++ (libprotobuf with protoc-generated classes; version not stated)
workload: Google Benchmark on one small message, Class{name, 3 x Student{id, name}} (45 bytes on the wire): encode into a 64-byte array and decode from a 45-byte buffer, protopuf vs protobuf SerializeToArray / ParseFromArray.
claimed_speedup: Per call: encode 17.2 ns (unsafe_mode) and 29.7 ns (safe_mode) vs protobuf 68.0 ns, about 4.0x and 2.3x faster; decode 188 ns (unsafe_mode) and 217 ns (safe_mode) vs protobuf 244 ns, about 1.30x and 1.12x faster (ratios derived from page data; times from the 'Before' table of PR #53).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the PR; the repo's CMake option ENABLE_BENCHMARK=ON expects a Release build
stars_or_usage: 207 stars; packaged in vcpkg and Conan Center (README badges)
tradeoffs: Messages are described as C++20 template types instead of .proto files (no code generator), so it needs GCC 11+, Clang 12+, MSVC 14.29+ or Apple Clang 17+ and compile times grow with templates; wire format is protobuf-compatible both ways. unsafe_mode skips bounds checks while safe_mode adds out-of-bounds checking and is slower. The README lists the supported field types but no benchmark section.
caveats: Numbers come from a contributor's pull-request comment (PR #53, opened July 2025, still unmerged) and not from the README, docs or CI, and the PR output omits the 'Run on' CPU lines, compiler, flags and protobuf version; the harness source is public (test/benchmark/main.cpp, added in PR #11, January 2021), so a rerun is possible but the published figures are not fully specified. The same PR's decode optimization (145 ns) was not merged because of a length-counting bug, so only the 'Before' figures are used. The message is tiny, and the protobuf decode loop constructs a new pb::Class per iteration (heap allocation for strings and the repeated field). The unsafe_mode rows skip bounds checks, so the headline encode ratio is with checks off; the safe_mode ratios are smaller. The repo README has no benchmark section and the protopuf.surge.sh docs were blocked (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so any numbers there were not seen.

name: utl::json (part of the UTL header-only library collection)
baseline: nlohmann::json (also PicoJSON; beats RapidJSON on serialization tasks only, loses to it on most parsing tasks)
workload: Parsing and serializing minimized/prettified JSON test files (strings.json, numbers.json, twitter.json, apache_builds.json, database.json) with a benchmark harness comparing utl::json, nlohmann, PicoJSON, and RapidJSON
claimed_speedup: ~2.2-2.4x faster parsing than nlohmann::json on twitter.json (402.89 vs 182.76 op/s) and apache_builds.json (2134.76 vs 881.03 op/s); ~1.9-2.4x faster serializing than nlohmann on the same files (e.g. twitter.json serialize: 834.42 vs 440.27 op/s); with a custom flat-map object type (not the library's default std::map), the author reports it 'beat RapidJSON on all serializing tasks' and closed most of the parsing gap on object-heavy database.json (all ratios derived from the page's relative-% table, which the page itself reports directly as percentages)

Not a universal win: on numbers.json and apache_builds.json, RapidJSON actually beats utl::json on parsing (128-172% relative i.e. faster); the win is consistent only vs nlohmann and PicoJSON.

name: cmp
baseline: msgpack-c (msgpack C API, v1.3.0 in the shootout)
workload: Encoding (write test) and incremental parsing of randomly generated schemaless data (2367-byte small and 248571-byte large MessagePack objects) in the ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks suite, with the hash cost subtracted.
claimed_speedup: No speed win exists. The project only says 'Fast, Lightweight, Flexible, and Robust' (no numbers). The independent shootout shows CMP v14 slower than msgpack C 1.3.0 on write: 7.33 us vs 6.42 us (small) and 660.19 us vs 544.24 us (large) on the AMD Phenom II X6 1090T desktop; 89.75 us vs 69.21 us (small) and 9206.05 us vs 8142.64 us (large) on a Raspberry Pi. CMP is the smallest MessagePack build on the desktop (3232 vs 4088 bytes for write) but not on the Raspberry Pi size build (2324 vs 1528 bytes).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3.0 on Arch Linux, -Wall -O3 -flto -fno-fat-lto-objects -DPIC -fPIC -DNDEBUG, each test run 7 times for 10 s, best and worst dropped

tradeoffs: No internal buffers and no heap allocation, about 4k lines in cmp.c/cmp.h, C89, user supplies read/write/skip callbacks (no growable buffer, no tree parser). Small and portable rather than fast.

name: bstring
baseline: C standard library char* string functions (strcpy, strcat, strchr, strstr, strcspn, memmove)
workload: Upstream Bstrlib's cbench.c example: operations per second for assignment, char extraction, scan, concatenation (250 appends of a 62 character string plus '!!' into one growing buffer) and replace, bstring C API against plain char* code. The same page also benchmarks upstream's C++ wrapper CBString against std::string with cppbench.cpp.
claimed_speedup: Bstrlib C API as percent of char* Clib speed (100% is parity), columns WATCOM C 11.0c / Visual C++ 6.0 / Intel C++ 6.0 / gcc 3.3.3 Cygwin / gcc 3.3.3 Power 4 SUSE: concatenation 21700% / 23700% / 21200% / 9260% / 3980%; assignment 182% / 198% / 218% / 89% / 91%; scan 214% / 125% / 159% / 209% / 89%; char extraction 95% / 96% / 101% / 102% / 113%; replace 147% / 114% / 125% / 101% / 86%. Same page, CBString over std::string: concatenation 187% (WATCOM + STL port), 21100% (Visual C++ 6.0), 19400% (Intel C++ 6.0), 1330% (g++ 3.3.3 Cygwin), 200% (g++ 3.3.3 Power 4); char extraction 63% to 132%; replace 95% to 144%.
compiler_and_flags: WATCOM C/C++ 11.0c, Visual C++ 6.0 (12.00.8168), Intel C++ 6.0 (4.0 99026), gcc 3.3.3 on Cygwin and on SUSE Linux. The page states only that the compiler must be set to 'a reasonable maximum performance setting'; the makefiles shipped in examples-09282006.zip use gcc -O3, MSVC /O2 and Intel /Ox /Ob2 but the page does not say these were the flags used.
hardware: Athlon XP 1.620GHz (all Windows/Cygwin columns); Power 4 1GHz (SUSE Linux column)
stars_or_usage: 175 stars (msteinert fork); upstream websnarf/bstrlib 570 stars; packaged in many distributions per the README's repology badge
tradeoffs: Length-prefixed string struct (slen, mlen, data) that stays NUL-terminated for interop with char* code, so length is O(1) and appends amortize, at the cost of a header and a different API from <string.h>. Dual licensed BSD-3-Clause or GPL-2.0 (user's choice). This fork is pure C: it removed upstream's C++ wrapper (CBString, bstrwrap) and the const_bstring type, and adds Meson build, Check tests, fuzzing and CI.
caveats: The numbers are for upstream Bstrlib (websnarf/bstrlib, last commit 2016-11-02), measured with 2000s era compilers on a 1.62GHz Athlon XP and a 1GHz Power 4; the msteinert fork is described as binary compatible but was not re-benchmarked, and the CBString versus std::string rows apply only to upstream because the fork dropped the C++ wrapper. First-party project page with percentages only (no raw ops/s), flags not stated for the run, so tier C. The large concatenation ratios come from the baseline calling strcat repeatedly on a growing buffer (rescanning the whole string every call, quadratic) while bstring tracks length; a C program that keeps its own length would not lose this much. In cbench.c the char* scan test searches TESTSTRING1 while the bstring scan test searches a different, shorter string ('Dot. 123. Some more data.'). The std::string comparison used old STLs (WATCOM STL port, Visual C++ 6.0, g++ 3.3.3 libstdc++) and resets the accumulator with accum = "", which those implementations may treat differently from CBString; std::string was faster or equal in several rows (char extraction 63-132%, replace 95-144%) and the C API loses on assignment and replace in some columns (89%, 91%, 86%). The fork's own README and comparisons.md claim 'improved overall performance of common string operations' and an advantage over std::string at least as large as the Str library's, with no numbers.

name: librope
baseline: flat contiguous string (a hand-written Rust String insert/delete by Unicode character offset, labelled 'Raw string'); the README itself says 'straight C strings' but gives no numbers for that
workload: Replaying real-world text-editing traces (automerge-paper, rustcode, sveltecomponent, seph-blog1 from josephg/crdt-benchmarks) as insert/delete operations at character offsets, measured as total replay time in ms; librope is called from Rust through FFI ('librope (C)' column).
claimed_speedup: README table of jumprope-rs, librope (C) vs Raw string: automerge-paper 16.28 ms vs 3908.13 ms; rustcode 3.93 ms vs 569.44 ms; sveltecomponent 1.59 ms vs 41.05 ms; seph-blog1 10.01 ms vs 1238.44 ms (about 240x, 145x, 26x and 124x faster, derived from page data). Same table: librope beats Ropey on all four (for example 16.28 ms vs 25.16 ms on automerge-paper) but is 2-3x slower than its Rust rewrite Jumprope (6.66 ms). librope's own README claims about 15 million edit operations per second and that inserts and deletes outperform straight C strings for any document longer than a few hundred bytes (no table for the C-string claim).
compiler_and_flags: Not fully stated. rope_benches README says to run `cargo run --release -- --bench` (criterion); the jumprope-rs Cargo.toml release profile has lto = true and codegen-units = 1; rope.c is built by the Rust `cc` crate from rope_benches/build.rs with no explicit flags; rustc and C compiler versions are not given.
hardware: A single core of a Ryzen 5800X (from the jumprope-rs README); OS and memory not stated.
tradeoffs: Skip-list rope over UTF-8; O(log n) insert and delete at character offsets, two files (rope.c, rope.h) to drop into a project. Compiling with -DROPE_WCHAR=1 for UTF-16 offset support costs about 35% throughput per its README. Heavier than a plain string for small documents (its README only claims a win for documents longer than a few hundred bytes). The author recommends the Rust rewrite Jumprope for new work.
caveats: First-party: the table lives in the README of the author's own Rust rewrite (jumprope-rs), where librope is a comparison column, not the subject. The 'Raw string' baseline is the author's own Rust String wrapper (rope_benches/src/edittablestr.rs) that finds the byte offset by scanning char_indices from the start on every edit, so the 25x-240x gaps mostly measure an O(n) character-offset scan on a flat string, not a tuned memmove-based std::string or C char buffer; the String row is commented out in the current rope_benches/src/main.rs ('takes a long time to run') and the realworld group loads data from a hard-coded /home/seph/... path, so the table is not reproducible out of the box. librope is driven through FFI with a CString allocation per insert, which handicaps it slightly. No libstdc++, libc++ or MSVC STL comparison and no C++ std::string or std::rope baseline appears anywhere (librope's own test/benchmark.c only runs the librope row, the 'c string' and SGI rope rows are disabled). The librope README's 15M ops/s link (home.seph.codes) is blocked from this environment, so it was not opened. Last commit October 2021; the author says the library works and points to Jumprope for newer work.

name: shoco
baseline: smaz (short-string compressor); also gzip and xz command-line tools
workload: Compress and decompress English words: all words in /usr/dict/share/words versus smaz, and /usr/share/dict/words (4,953,680 bytes) compressed as one file with the included shoco command-line tool versus gzip and xz.
claimed_speedup: README: shoco 'is typically faster by at least a factor of 2' than smaz; example 0.325s (smaz, 28% average compression) versus 0.145s (shoco, 33% average compression) for compress plus decompress of all words in /usr/dict/share/words (about 2.2x, derived from page data). Versus gzip and xz on /usr/share/dict/words: shoco 0.070s compress / 0.010s decompress / 3,393,975 bytes; gzip 0.470s / 0.048s / 1,476,083 bytes (6.7x and 4.8x faster, derived from page data); xz 3.300s / 0.148s / 1,229,980 bytes (47x and 15x faster, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Entropy coder for short ASCII strings built on a compiled-in bigram model (default model tuned for English words; a Python script generates new models from your own data). Compression ratio is far worse than gzip or xz on larger inputs (3.39 MB versus 1.48 MB and 1.23 MB on the 4.95 MB word list); output never grows for plain ASCII input but non-ASCII input can; copy-in C files (shoco.c, shoco.h, shoco_model.h), no packaging.
caveats: First-party numbers measured 'on my computer': no CPU, compiler, flags or OS version stated, no timing method or run count, and the smaz row has no committed harness. The gzip/xz table times the shoco command-line tool on one whole 4.95 MB file, which the README itself calls 'not a strong point of shoco', so it does not measure the short-string use case, and gzip/xz are generic compressors with much better ratios, so the speed comparison is not like for like. The baseline is not a C++ standard facility. The README begins 'This project is unmaintained. You should use ZStandard nowadays'; the last code changes in the commit list are from 2015 (merge of pull request #17 on 2015-12-08), and the 2026-02-16 commit is titled 'project is unmaintained'. A third-party benchmark snippet found by search covers a Go port (tmthrgd/shoco), not this C code, and was not opened.

name: CDRC atomic_weak_ptr (concurrent_deferred_rc)
baseline: just::thread's atomic<weak_ptr> (commercial third-party implementation of the C++20 std::atomic<std::weak_ptr> interface)
workload: Ramalethe & Correia lock-free concurrent doubly-linked queue using atomic weak back-pointers; P threads repeatedly pop-then-reinsert an element, P = 1 to 192, on a 4-socket 72-core machine
claimed_speedup: 67x faster than just::thread at P=1 thread; 4.2x faster at P=8 threads; ~10x faster at P=192 threads (own weak-pointer implementation is 19-33% slower than a hand-customized manual-memory-management baseline over the same range) (paper Fig. 12)

tradeoffs: Requires a C++20-concepts-capable compiler; full benchmark reproduction needs jemalloc + NUMA-aware setup; library is research-grade (from the CDRC/acquire-retire papers), not a drop-in std::shared_ptr replacement, and uses more memory than manual reclamation in oversubscribed scenarios.
caveats: The quoted numbers compare against just::thread, a commercial library implementing the std::atomic<weak_ptr> interface, not against libstdc++/libc++'s own atomic<weak_ptr> (which those stdlibs did not implement at the time); MSVC STL is the only mainstream stdlib with a native implementation and was not the one benchmarked here. Paper also reports a separate 2-3x throughput gain over prior concurrent-refcounting implementations (not vs std::shared_ptr directly).

name: Indiesort (plf::indiesort)
workload: Sorting vectors or arrays of large structs (496 bytes) with plf::indiesort, which sorts an index/pointer array and then permutes the elements, versus direct std::sort; also sorting std::list contents versus std::list::sort for types under 272 bytes; averaged across all numbers of sorted elements.
claimed_speedup: +146% faster than std::sort on vectors or arrays of large structs (496 bytes), on average across all numbers of sorted elements; crossover is any type larger than 152 bytes. +28% faster than std::list's internal sort on types smaller than 272 bytes.
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++98 through C++20 compatible. Temporary memory of N * (sizeof(pointer) + sizeof(size_t)) for non-random-access ranges and N * sizeof(U) for random-access ranges (U is the smallest unsigned type able to hold N). Not a win for small types: std::sort is faster on vectors and arrays below 152 bytes, and std::list's own sort is faster for types above 272 bytes. Its main use is letting std::sort-style algorithms run on non-random-access containers.
caveats: First-party README numbers only. The README gives no compiler, flags, CPU, or element counts; the benchmark page at plflib.org/indiesort.htm was EGRESS_BLOCKED in this session, so the methodology could not be checked. A web search snippet from older pages quotes '+130% ... vector with 496 byte structs' (and '~480 bytes'), so the headline figure has moved between releases (README now says +146%). The win only exists for large or non-trivially-movable element types, so the average depends on which sizes the benchmark includes (not stated). The baseline standard library (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC STL) is not stated.

name: swenson/sort (sort.h)
workload: Sorting 10,000 random int64_t values (lrand48) once per routine with demo.c, timed with gettimeofday, against libc qsort with a function-pointer comparator.
claimed_speedup: quick sort 579 us vs stdlib qsort 1285 us per 10,000 int64_t (about 2.2x, derived from page data); heap sort 592 us, in-place merge sort 903 us, merge sort 999 us, tim sort 1005 us are also faster than qsort 1285 us; stdlib mergesort 1299 us and heapsort 2109 us are slower than qsort
compiler_and_flags: Unstated for the README numbers. The Makefile default is CFLAGS ?= -O3 -g -Wall -std=c89 -pedantic -Wno-long-long -Wno-format with CC ?= gcc, which may differ from the README run.
hardware: 2014-era MacBook Pro (CPU model unstated)
tradeoffs: Single C89 header that generates type-specialised routines through #define SORT_TYPE, SORT_NAME and SORT_CMP, so each instantiation adds code size. Comparator inlining is the source of the win over qsort. Includes stable options (timsort, merge sort, grail sort, sqrt sort). Not a C++ std::sort drop-in. The default demo comparator (x - y) is unsafe for integers whose difference can overflow.
caveats: The README table comes from one run (RUNS is 1 in demo.c) of one 10,000-element array on an unnamed 2014 laptop, with compiler and flags unstated. The baseline is C qsort calling through a function pointer, not std::sort or an inlined-comparator sort, so the gap measures comparator inlining more than algorithm quality. Only quick sort, heap sort and in-place merge sort show a clear win; the README itself says results depend on the machine and data. benchmark.c in the repo (100,000 elements, 1 s loops) is more careful but no results from it are published. stdlib heapsort and mergesort rows exist only on non-Linux platforms.

name: Timsort (gfx::timsort, cpp-TimSort)
baseline: std::sort and std::stable_sort (also std::inplace_merge for gfx::timmerge)
workload: Sorting 100000-element int and std::string sequences that are randomized, reversed or already sorted; merging two sorted runs of 100000 elements for int and std::string.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark (timing scale: sec., size 100000): reversed int std::sort 0.045461 vs timsort 0.019139 (about 2.4x faster, derived from page data); sorted int 0.021876 vs 0.008042 (about 2.7x, derived); reversed std::string 0.586707 vs 0.345099 (about 1.7x, derived); sorted std::string 0.402458 vs 0.298639 (about 1.3x, derived); against std::stable_sort, reversed int 0.575431 vs 0.019139 (about 30x, derived). On randomized data timsort is SLOWER: int std::sort 0.695253 vs timsort 1.255825, std::string 3.438217 vs 5.791845. Merge benchmark (ms): sorted std::string std::inplace_merge 158.238114 vs timmerge 0.273858 (about 578x, derived), reversed int 11.441404 vs 4.017482, randomized int 33.404430 vs 37.047990 (timmerge slower).
compiler_and_flags: Sort run: Apple LLVM 7.0.0 (clang-700.0.72), c++ -Wall -Wextra -g -DNDEBUG -O2 -std=c++11 example/bench.cpp. Merge run: GCC 10.2.0 on Linux (Manjaro per the wiki page), c++ -Wall -Wextra -g -DNDEBUG -O2 -std=c++11 bench_merge.cpp. Standard libraries inferred from the toolchains (Apple clang on darwin uses libc++, GCC on Linux uses libstdc++), not stated.
hardware: CPU model not stated (target x86_64-apple-darwin14.5.0 for the sort run, x86_64-pc-linux-gnu for the merge run)
stars_or_usage: 319 stars; on Conan Center as timsort
tradeoffs: Stable O(n log n) sort that needs extra heap memory and cannot fall back to an O(n log^2 n) in-place algorithm when allocation is short. Slower than std::sort on random data. Version 3.x requires C++20 (ranges, projections); branches 2.x.y (C++11) and 1.x.y (C++03) are no longer actively maintained.
caveats: Tier C: the project's own benchmark code with no CPU model and no standard-library statement. The README sort output was produced with Apple LLVM 7.0.0 (2015 toolchain) at -O2 and the README states plainly that timsort is slower than std::ranges::sort on randomized sequences and faster only on partially-sorted ones, so the win is limited to presorted, reversed or nearly sorted inputs (the awesome-cpp listing says the same). The sort numbers come from the old C++11 example/bench.cpp, not necessarily the current benchmarks directory built with -DBUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON. Baseline is std::sort for the 'faster' rows, which is not stable; the fair stable baseline is std::stable_sort (also beaten on reversed and sorted input, and also slower on random input). The repo moved from gfx/cpp-TimSort to timsort/cpp-TimSort; the old URL redirects. The wiki page for the merge benchmark (https://github.com/timsort/cpp-TimSort/wiki/Benchmark-results) lists only the representative rows and GCC 10.2.0 / Manjaro / x86_64 with no CPU model.
found_via: seed-record pass: lead page https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Sorting (listing says 'outperforms quicksort-based algorithms including std::sort, for reversed or semi-sorted data'), then the repo README at https://github.com/timsort/cpp-TimSort and its wiki Benchmark-results page

name: voracious_radix_sort
workload: In-memory sort of i64 (and other primitive-type) arrays at sizes from 100 to 1000+ elements across ~25 synthetic distributions (uniform, +-1e9 range, ascending/descending +variants, Zipf, normal, sqrt, pipe organ, etc.), 5 iterations, single- and multi-threaded, run on the maintainer's own machine and checked into the repo's results/ directory
claimed_speedup: i64, 1000 elements, uniform distribution: Rust Std (stable sort) avg 36.525us vs Voracious (unstable/stable trait) avg 23.334us, ~1.56x faster (derived from page data); README states it is 'way faster than Rust standard sort and Rust unstable sort... on most types and data distributions', with radix sort's advantage expected to grow on the larger arrays it targets

caveats: This compares against Rust's own std::sort/sort_unstable, not C++ std::sort directly, so compared_against_cpp_std_directly=false and baseline_stdlib is empty; the project's own benchmark methodology doesn't state optimization flags for this run, capping it at tier C; the quoted 1.56x figure is for a small (1000-element) array, which is below the size where radix sort is expected to shine according to the project's own docs

name: glibc (libc string functions, qsort, regexec, strtod, malloc)
baseline: musl libc (the copy bundled with zig 0.15.2, statically linked)
workload: 32 libc micro-benchmarks (benchmark.c), each calibrated to a target run time and reported as ns per call: strncmp, strcpy, strncpy, strstr, strchr, qsort of 4096 ints, regexec of an e-mail pattern over 128 lines, strtod over 256 numbers, malloc/free small and medium, printf family, file I/O, and others.
claimed_speedup: glibc fastest in 17 of 32 rows (musl 2, musl+jemalloc 11, 2 ties); README summary: 'glibc wins most benchmarks'. ns/op, glibc vs musl: strncmp 9.91 vs 366.91; strcpy 22.05 vs 129.35; strncpy 25.20 vs 136.77; strstr_search 36.28 vs 104.23; strtod_parse 52.40 vs 226.72 (4.3x, derived from page data); regex_match 117.54 vs 694.23 (5.9x, derived from page data); qsort_int 214387.15 vs 591408.11 (2.8x, derived from page data); malloc_free_small 10.78 vs 122.61; malloc_free_medium 828.38 vs 3343.75. musl is faster on atoi_parse 3.96 vs 9.28, bsearch_int 10.52 vs 16.02, strtok_parse, strrchr 157.31 vs 354.19 and memcpy 154.19 vs 4043.27; musl+jemalloc beats glibc malloc_free_medium 80.59 vs 828.38.
compiler_and_flags: zig 0.15.2 (zig cc, clang 20.1.2); -std=c11 -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto=full -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops -DNDEBUG -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math -g0 -s; targets x86_64-linux-gnu and x86_64-linux-musl (run.sh)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U with Radeon Graphics; Linux 6.8.0-87-generic (Ubuntu 22.04 kernel); run 2025-11-18
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars (unofficial bminor/glibc mirror); the default libc of most Linux distributions
tradeoffs: LGPL: the normal route is dynamic linking, static linking brings LGPL obligations and breaks NSS and iconv loading. Much larger runtime than musl. The comparison is for x86-64 on one CPU; glibc's speed on str*/mem* routines depends on per-CPU variant selection (general knowledge, not shown on the benchmark page). malloc is the default ptmalloc2 and loses to jemalloc on the medium-size row.
caveats: Third-party hobby repo (7 stars, 7 commits, no licence file shown), one machine, one calibrated run per benchmark with no repeats or variance. glibc version is not stated: the binary is built with zig cc -target x86_64-linux-gnu and runs against the host's own glibc (host looks like Ubuntu 22.04, so probably 2.35, an inference). The musl side is compiled by zig from its bundled musl source (version and zig's libc optimisation level not stated) and linked statically, while glibc is the distro's prebuilt dynamic library, so the two sides are built differently. Several rows are not meaningful: strlen, strcmp and memcmp show about 0.1 ns/op (pure calls hoisted out of the loop, ties), the memcpy row has glibc 26x slower than musl (4043.27 vs 154.19, looks like a harness artifact), and the strstr haystack is cut to about 16 KB because the strcpy that plants the first marker writes a NUL (read from benchmark.c). A second vendor blog (BellSoft Alpaquita, which sells a musl build with tuned routines) reports glibc ahead of musl on memcpy and memcmp; the page was EGRESS_BLOCKED here and its numbers are not used. repo_url is the read-only mirror (archived 2026-02-15, last commit 2026-01-20); upstream development continues at sourceware.org, which was not opened. Baseline is a C library, not a C++ standard library.

name: HighwayHash
workload: Hash inputs of 8, 31, 32, 63, 64, and 1024 bytes on a single idle core of a Xeon E5-2690 v3 (2.6GHz), comparing HighwayHashAVX2/SSE41 against SipHash, SipHash13, SipTreeHash and SipTreeHash13, measured in cycles/byte with a custom cycle-accurate nanobenchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: At 1024 bytes: HighwayHashAVX2 0.24 cycles/byte vs SipHash 1.26 cycles/byte -> ~5.25x faster (derived from page data, matching the README's own '5x faster' claim); at 64 bytes: HighwayHashAVX2 0.95 vs SipHash 1.93 -> ~2x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: A patched GCC 4.9, 64-bit build (per README's 'Speed measurements' section)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3, 2.6 GHz, single idle core
tradeoffs: SIMD-dependent (AVX2/SSE4.1/VSX), needs runtime CPU dispatch for portability; the hash output is explicitly declared 'frozen forever' so no further algorithmic improvements will ever land; repository is archived by Google (read-only) so no future compiler/security fixes.
caveats: Compared against SipHash/SipTreeHash, not std::hash. Benchmark used a 'patched' GCC 4.9 (a roughly decade-old, non-stock compiler) on hardware from ~2014-2015, and Google archived the repository in 2024, so these numbers do not reflect modern compilers or CPUs.

name: komihash
workload: Hash short keys (0-15 bytes, 8-28 bytes) and 256,000-byte bulk buffers, averaged across 10 compiler/CPU combinations (GCC 11.5, Clang 18/19, ICC 19, clang-cl 18, Apple Clang 15) on Ryzen 3700X/9950X, Xeon E-2386G, Core i7-7700K, and Apple M1, measuring cycles/hash and GB/s.
claimed_speedup: Averaged over all 10 combos: komihash 5.34 needs ~7.2 cycles/hash (0-15b) and ~8.6 cycles/hash (8-28b) vs wyhash_final4's 13.5/18.0 and XXH3_64's 14.2/21.8 -- roughly 1.9-2x fewer cycles on short keys (derived from page data). On 256KB bulk hashing the result is mixed: komihash reaches up to 42.7 GB/s but XXH3_64 reaches up to 68.4 GB/s on some platforms, so komihash's advantage is specific to short/medium keys, not bulk throughput.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5.0 (-O3 -msse2 / -O3 -mavx2), LLVM Clang 19.1.7 (-O3 -mavx2), clang-cl 18.1.8 (/Ox -msse2 or -mavx2), ICC 19.0 (/O3 /QxSSE2), Apple Clang 15.0.0 (-O3) -- full 10-combo matrix given in the README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3700X (4.2GHz) and Ryzen 9950X (5.7GHz), Intel Xeon E-2386G (5.1GHz), Core i7-7700K (4.5GHz), Apple M1 (3.5GHz)
tradeoffs: Non-cryptographic hash, not adversarial-collision-resistant without seeding; header-only C (compiles as C++) but exposes plain C functions (komihash(), komirand()) rather than a std::hash<T> specialization, so it needs a small wrapper to drop into unordered_map/unordered_set.
caveats: Never benchmarked against std::hash itself -- std::hash for strings in libstdc++/libc++ is a different, generally weaker-quality hash, so this evidence is against best-in-class non-cryptographic hashes (xxHash, wyhash), not literally the requested std::hash baseline. Numbers are the author's own benchmark (first-party), though the methodology (10 compiler/CPU combinations, exact flags) is unusually complete for a first-party result.

name: MUM/VMUM hash
baseline: xxHash3, Google CityHash (City64), Bob Jenkins SpookyHash, SipHash24, MetroHash, t1ha2 — widely-used non-cryptographic hash functions used in place of std::hash for hash-table keys
workload: Hashing 1,280M keys of lengths from 3 to 1024 bytes, plus 10,000 x 16MB bulk keys, on four different machines; each measurement repeated 3x and the minimum time kept.
claimed_speedup: Geomean of relative throughput across key lengths, VMUM-V2 normalized to 1.00 (higher/lower time = slower/faster): on Apple M4, VMUM-V2 is ~1.3x faster than xxHash3 (ratio 0.79), ~2.6x faster than CityHash (0.38), and ~4.8x faster than SipHash24 (0.21); on IBM Power10 it's roughly on par with xxHash3 (0.93) and ~2.1x faster than CityHash (0.48). (derived from page data: the README's per-length tables list ratio+time for VMUM-V1/V2, MUM-V3/V4, Spooky, City, xxHash3, t1ha2, SipHash24 and Metro on AMD Ryzen 9900X, an Intel chip, IBM Power10 and Apple M4.)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.1 (AMD Ryzen 9900X and Apple M4), GCC 12.3.1 (Intel machine), GCC 11.5.0 (IBM Power10); -O3 for all; -flto added only for the competing hash functions (not MUM/VMUM) to allow cross-file inlining, after complaints that the original comparison didn't inline competitors.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9900X, an Intel Core i5 (13th-gen class), IBM Power10, Apple M4 (10-core Mac mini)
tradeoffs: VMUM needs target SIMD (AVX2 on x86-64, NEON on aarch64, Altivec on ppc64) to get its full speed advantage on mid/long keys, falling back to scalar emulation elsewhere; an earlier VMUM/MUM-V3 had a collision-attack weakness (fixed Nov 2025 at ~10% extra cost, now default); requires compiler support for 128-bit integer extensions.
caveats: No LICENSE file exists in the repository and `gh api` reports no SPDX license, so legal reuse of the code is unclear even though it is public and the author (a GCC/GNU contributor) documents it thoroughly. The benchmark is first-party (author's own repo and graphs), not third-party verified, though it discloses compiler, flags, hardware and methodology in full, meeting the bar for Tier A.

baseline: std::strstr / libc strstr (same problem as std::string::find and the default std::search)

claimed_speedup: std::strstr: 0.662s vs AVX2 (generic) kernel: 0.364s -> ~1.82x faster (derived from page data); SSE2 (generic): 0.489s -> ~1.35x faster (derived from page data). Other machines in the results folder (Haswell, Cascade Lake, Knights Landing, ARMv7/ARMv8) show similar or larger gaps.

name: Boost.Algorithm Boyer-Moore / Boyer-Moore-Horspool searchers
workload: Locate an ~105 or ~43-character pattern (present in the middle/end, or absent) inside a 2,756,252-character random 8-bit text corpus, using boost::algorithm::boyer_moore_search / boyer_moore_horspool_search vs std::search, via the Boost.Algorithm search_test2 benchmark tool.
claimed_speedup: std::search: 0.4848s (100%, baseline) vs boyer_moore_search: 0.1171s (24.16%) vs boyer_moore_horspool_search: 0.1076s (22.2%) for a 105-char pattern found mid-corpus -- i.e. boyer_moore ~4.1x faster, boyer_moore_horspool ~4.5x faster than std::search (derived from page data; percentages are verbatim from the PR). A second case (91-char 'not found' pattern) shows std::search 1.028s vs boyer_moore_horspool 0.1825s (~5.6x, derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; boyer_moore_search/boyer_moore_horspool_search ship in mainline Boost.Algorithm and are used wherever Boost is deployed
tradeoffs: Boyer-Moore/Horspool searchers build an O(alphabet + pattern) skip table before searching, which pays off when reused or on longer patterns but adds overhead for a single tiny one-off search; since C++17 the same two algorithms are also standardized as std::boyer_moore_searcher / std::boyer_moore_horspool_searcher, usable directly with std::search -- so on a C++17+ toolchain the standard library itself can close most of this gap without Boost.
caveats: The quoted numbers come from Marshall Clow's (Boost.Algorithm's maintainer) still-open, unmerged PR #25 (from 2016, proposing an additional Musser-Nishanov searcher); the timing table is for the already-mainline boyer_moore/boyer_moore_horspool searchers, not the unmerged musser_nishanov code. Compiler, flags, and CPU model are not stated in the PR, so treat the ~4-5x figures as indicative rather than reproducible as-is; the author notes run-to-run variance of 5-10%.
found_via: WebSearch: "faster than std::search" OR "beats std::search" C++ benchmark github -> github.com/boostorg/algorithm/pull/25

name: CityHash
baseline: MurmurHash2/MurmurHash3 (Murmur2, Murmur3F, Murmur3A) — widely-used non-cryptographic hash functions used in place of std::hash
workload: Hashing short strings (1, 8, 64 bytes) and long strings, on a single core of a 2.67GHz Intel Xeon X5550.
claimed_speedup: CityHash64 v1.0.3: 7ns for 1 byte vs Murmur2's 6ns (Murmur2 slightly faster here) but 9ns for 64 bytes vs Murmur2's 15ns and Murmur3F's 23ns (roughly 1.7x-2.5x faster at 64 bytes, derived from page data). CityHashCrc256 peaks at about 5-5.5 bytes/cycle on long strings vs the fastest Murmur variant (Murmur3F) at about 2.4 bytes/cycle (roughly 2x-2.3x faster, derived from page data).
hardware: Single core, 2.67GHz Intel Xeon X5550
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars; historically used in many hash-table/database implementations before Google's own successors (FarmHash, Abseil's hash) superseded it
tradeoffs: No incremental/streaming API; not SIMD/AVX-optimized the way modern hashes (xxh3, rapidhash) are; the CRC-based variants depend on the _mm_crc32_u64 intrinsic being available.
caveats: Repository is archived by Google and had its last real commit in 2022; the README's benchmark numbers date to roughly the CityHash v1.0.3/1.1 era (~2011) on now-obsolete server hardware, do not state compiler flags, and are not compared against any modern hash (xxh3, rapidhash, wyhash); tier capped at C because compiler/flags are unstated for these specific numbers.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): surfaced while cataloguing hash-function shootout history referenced from rurban/smhasher and rapidhash's README, in response to the seed query 'hash function benchmark std::hash comparison'.

name: RapidFuzz
workload: Fuzzy string scorers (ratio, partial_ratio, token_sort_ratio, token_set_ratio, partial_token_sort_ratio, partial_token_set_ratio, QRatio, WRatio) over 10,000 random strings of length 10 (ASCII letters and digits) against 100 samples drawn from that list, reported as word pairs evaluated per second, once calling the scorer per pair from Python and once through cdist.
claimed_speedup: Scorer called directly from Python, pairs per second RapidFuzz vs FuzzyWuzzy: ratio 6,206,379 vs 480,115 (12.9x), partial_ratio 3,091,339 vs 212,794 (14.5x), token_sort_ratio 3,155,091 vs 151,101 (20.9x), token_set_ratio 1,590,972 vs 108,940 (14.6x), partial_token_sort_ratio 1,767,978 vs 105,151 (16.8x), partial_token_set_ratio 1,213,823 vs 81,875 (14.8x), QRatio 5,231,998 vs 184,591 (28.3x), WRatio 1,264,866 vs 59,436 (21.3x). Through cdist: ratio 135,463,598 vs 525,021 (258x), token_sort_ratio 120,274,547 vs 167,720 (717x), QRatio 126,989,691 vs 204,064 (622x), partial_ratio 12,936,872 vs 183,338 (71x), WRatio 2,516,289 vs 63,982 (39x). Ratios are derived from page data (chart labels).
stars_or_usage: 377 stars (rapidfuzz-cpp); the Python package rapidfuzz/RapidFuzz that vendors it has 4.2k+ stars
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ library (CMake target rapidfuzz::rapidfuzz) with Levenshtein, Indel, LCSseq, Jaro-Winkler and FuzzyWuzzy-style fuzz scorers plus cached scorers for one-query-many-choices use. The extract/extractOne/cdist 'process' layer exists only in the Python package; the C++ README shows a few lines to write the equivalents (and an OpenMP loop for parallelism). Results are meant to match FuzzyWuzzy's.
caveats: The only numeric comparison I could reach is the Python package's README chart (docs/img/scorer.svg and cdist.svg, also on the RapidFuzz README), whose labels I read by rendering the SVG; it measures the Python wrapper RapidFuzz (which pulls rapidfuzz-cpp in as extern/ submodule) against pure-Python FuzzyWuzzy, not C++ against a C++ baseline, and nothing compares rapidfuzz-cpp itself with std::string code. The cdist numbers add batching (and possibly threading) that the C++ library does not provide by itself, so the 258x to 717x figures overstate the per-pair algorithmic gain. Python version, FuzzyWuzzy version, compiler, flags and CPU are not stated; the chart was generated 2021-09-10 (Matplotlib metadata) and the headline numbers are old. rapidfuzz-cpp's own bench/ directory (Google Benchmark files bench-fuzz, bench-levenshtein, bench-lcs, bench-jarowinkler) only times RapidFuzz against itself, and the README's detailed Benchmarks.md link is a 404 (rapidfuzz.github.io docs are blocked here). The seed's guessed baseline std::string does not apply.

name: ICU (ICU4C collation)
baseline: glibc strcoll (glibc 2.12.3 in the ICU4C 3.8 chart, glibc 2.13 in the ICU4C 4.8 chart)
workload: String comparison (strcoll), sort key generation (keygen) and sort key length (keylen) of an ICU4C RuleBasedCollator with default options against glibc, over a large list of language-specific names, each operation repeated 1000 times, per locale.
claimed_speedup: en_US with Latin test data: strcoll 199%, keygen 77%, keylen 99% in ICU4C's favour (chart convention: positive means ICU4C better); ja_JP strcoll 421% in ICU4C's favour (snippet only, which chart not identified).
tradeoffs: Large library with its own data tables; UTF-16 is its native string form; ICU4C offers C and C++ APIs; Unicode-3.0 license (older releases used the ICU license).
caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: icu.unicode.org, the PostgreSQL mailing list and lists.gnupg.org are EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so the numbers come from WebSearch result text, not an opened page; percentages are chart deltas, not ratios, and the chart's platform, CPU and compiler fields were not readable. Charts are old: ICU4C 3.8 versus glibc 2.12.3 and ICU4C 4.8 versus glibc 2.13 (about 2008 to 2011); both libraries have changed since. The chart page itself warns results vary with hardware and compiler and that strcoll is sensitive to code alignment (10% swings). The benchmark code is public (icu4c/source/test/perf/collationperf/collperf.cpp in unicode-org/icu, which 'compar[es] collation performance and key lengths of ICU, Windows native collation and Unix/POSIX collation') but no committed results were found. A second snippet-only claim: a PostgreSQL mailing-list message reports ICU normalization at 0.861 s and 0.651 s against PostgreSQL's built-in 4.024 s and 6.655 s on two conversions (hardware and method unknown). The guessed baseline 'standard UTF-8 processing' does not match any evidence; this is a collation and normalization claim. ICU is also the incumbent that other Unicode libraries benchmark against.

name: micron.cpp (cmemory memcpy/memset/memmove)
baseline: glibc memcpy / memset / memmove (system libc, called as ::memcpy in the harness; glibc version not stated)
workload: benches/memory_random_bench.cpp: batches of 16384 random-offset operations with SPEC2017 size and alignment distributions over a working set of 32 KiB to 1 MiB, 5 measurements, CPU pinned, cycles per byte; micron mc::memcpy/memset/memmove versus libc.
claimed_speedup: benches/results/mem_random_s2_final.csv cycles/byte micron vs libc: memcpy 0.2803 vs 0.3480 at 32768 (1.24x, derived from page data), 0.2590 vs 0.3815 at 262144 (1.47x, derived), 0.3045 vs 0.4829 at 1048576 (1.59x, derived); memset 0.2377 vs 0.4532 at 1048576 (1.91x, derived), 0.1936 vs 0.2190 at 32768 (1.13x, derived); memmove 0.3236 vs 0.4231 at 1048576 (1.31x, derived). micron is faster in all 18 rows of that file.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the CSV. Sibling result files from the same author and dates (abcmalloc_core_baseline.csv, rng_final_native.csv) state GCC 16.2.1 20260819, -O3 -march=native, built with 'duck --perf --fp --no-ssp --no-lto -i .'. The bench source adds #pragma GCC optimize(-fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns).
hardware: Not stated in the CSV. Sibling result files name an Intel Core i7-5960X (Haswell-E, 8C/16T, 20 MiB L3), Linux 7.1.9-200.fc44 (Fedora 44), CPU pinned.
tradeoffs: Freestanding re-implementation of libc and the C++ standard library (no libc dependency, C++23 or C++26, x86-64 focus with an ARM32 and bare-metal branch); README states the ABI may change without notice, performance takes precedence over safety, and the code is not a drop-in for the STL ABI. abcmalloc, the bundled allocator, is MIT while the rest is BSL-1.0.
caveats: The README and docs publish no numbers; the 'must demonstrate superior performance' line is a design principle. Only the benches/results directory has data, and the only micron-versus-external-baseline rows found are memory primitives against glibc, not the allocator or STL containers named in the seed guess (allocator results are before/after against micron's own earlier revisions, and sort_bench_std.cpp, heap_bench_std.cpp and stack_bench_std.cpp have no recorded results). The claim is selective: the sibling file mem_detail_s2_final_a.csv (same author) shows libc faster overall for hot memcpy (micron wins 170 of 513 cells, geomean libc/micron cycles 0.96) and hot memmove (45 of 182, 0.89), faster on all 14 cold-cache memcpy cells (0.85) and on 11 of 14 cold memset cells, with libc far ahead at tiny sizes (for example memmove at 3 bytes 0.27 vs 1.12 cycles/byte); micron wins hot memset (222 of 386, geomean 1.12). The random-size win applies to working sets of 32 KiB and above only. First-party, single machine (Haswell-E, an older CPU than glibc's newest ifunc tuning targets), glibc version unstated, compiler and CPU absent from the cited CSV, so tier C. Ratios are derived from page data.

name: netbsd-curses
workload: Build and install of the library, programs, shared and static libs and headers (make -j2 all install) on a dual-core x86_64 sabotage Linux system with built-in terminfo and widechar support.
claimed_speedup: README Table 1: build time (make -j2) 59 sec for ncurses vs 9 sec for netbsd curses (6.6x, derived from page data); installed size 15.9 MB vs 1.3 MB; size of libncursesw.so 346 KB vs 150 KB; extracted source 15.8 MB vs 3.3 MB; static-linked nano 334 KB vs 288 KB.
compiler_and_flags: CFLAGS '-g0 -fdata-sections -ffunction-sections -Os -fno-unwind-tables -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -Wa,--noexecstack', LDFLAGS '-s -Wl,--gc-sections -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now' (README Appendix A); compiler not named
hardware: dual-core x86_64 sabotage Linux system (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Close to a drop-in ncurses replacement with widechar support, but no mouse handling (no-op macros), only 510 color pairs, missing rarely used functions such as vidputs(), different struct layout (some programs such as Python's curses module need patches), curses and terminfo are split into libcurses and libterminfo, and terminfo is a CDB database.
caveats: The claim is build time and footprint, not runtime curses performance; no runtime benchmark against ncurses was found. Single run, no repeats or variance, ncurses and netbsd-curses versions not stated, and the configure-heavy ncurses build is single-threaded for part of its time (the README says netbsd curses should scale better with more jobs, which is untested). Binary size table is a size-optimised (-Os) build. First-party numbers, no benchmark script in the repo.
